blocks.content:
Before touching transformations, the predictors and the labels are separated — `drop()` on the target column creates a copy, leaving the original training set untouched, and the label column is copied out on its own. This matters because the label should generally not go through the same feature transformations as the inputs.

Most ML algorithms simply cannot handle missing values, and this dataset has some in `total_bedrooms`. There are three general options: drop the affected rows, drop the whole attribute, or fill (impute) the gaps with some value like zero, the mean, or the median. Dropping is destructive and throws away potentially useful rows or a whole feature, so filling the gaps (imputation) is the least destructive choice; this chapter fills them with the median.

Rather than compute the median with plain Pandas, Scikit-Learn's `SimpleImputer` is the better tool, because it *remembers* the value it computed — its `fit()` step learns and stores each column's median, and that stored value can then be reapplied consistently to the validation set, the test set, and any brand-new data the model sees later, so nothing is imputed with a different reference value than what training used. Since a median only makes sense for numeric columns, the imputer is fit only on the numeric subset of the data (excluding the one text column), and it's applied to *all* numeric attributes, not just the one currently missing values, since future data could have gaps anywhere.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy="median")
housing_num = housing.select_dtypes(include=[np.number])
imputer.fit(housing_num)
X = imputer.transform(housing_num)
```

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Why is it better to use SimpleImputer than to just call housing[col].fillna(housing[col].median()) directly?

blocks.content:
Scikit-Learn's whole library holds together because every object plays one of a few consistent roles, and once you know the vocabulary, a new class in the library is rarely a mystery. An **estimator** is anything that can learn (estimate) parameters from data — `SimpleImputer` is one, since fitting it means computing and storing a median. The `fit()` method always does the learning, and it takes the dataset (plus, for supervised algorithms, the labels too); any extra setting that isn't learned from data but instead configures *how* learning happens (like `SimpleImputer`'s `strategy` argument) is a hyperparameter, set through the constructor before fitting ever runs.

A **transformer** is an estimator that can also transform data — its `transform()` method takes a dataset and hands back a modified one, typically using whatever it learned during `fit()`. Every transformer also gets a convenience `fit_transform()` for free, which just chains the two steps (sometimes faster than calling them separately). A **predictor**, by contrast, is an estimator that can make predictions — it exposes `predict()`, and usually a `score()` method to judge prediction quality against labeled data.

A few more conventions round this out: hyperparameters and learned parameters are both exposed as plain public attributes (learned ones get a trailing underscore, like `imputer.statistics_`); datasets are represented as ordinary NumPy arrays or SciPy sparse matrices rather than custom container classes; and sensible defaults mean most classes work reasonably well out of the box, without exhaustive configuration.

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: What is the difference between a transformer and a predictor in Scikit-Learn's vocabulary?

blocks.content:
The one text column in this dataset, ocean proximity, only ever takes on a handful of repeated values, which makes it a categorical attribute rather than free text — and most ML algorithms want numbers, not strings, as input. `OrdinalEncoder` is the simplest fix: it assigns each distinct category an integer. But that introduces a subtle and often wrong assumption: an algorithm reading those integers will treat category 0 and category 1 as *closer* than category 0 and category 4, purely because of the numbers assigned, even when there's no real ordering to the categories at all. That's fine for genuinely ordered categories ("bad", "average", "good") but wrong for something like ocean proximity, where the categories have no natural rank.

The standard fix is **one-hot encoding**: create one binary column per category, each equal to 1 exactly when a row belongs to that category and 0 otherwise — only one column is ever "hot" per row. `OneHotEncoder` does this and, because the resulting matrix is mostly zeros for datasets with many categories, returns a memory-efficient sparse matrix by default rather than a dense array.

Pandas has its own `get_dummies()` that looks similar, but it lacks a crucial property: it only knows about the categories present in whatever DataFrame you pass it, so a batch of new data missing a category (or containing an unfamiliar one) produces a *different* set of output columns than training did — a silent mismatch that would corrupt a live model. `OneHotEncoder`, once fitted, remembers the exact categories it was trained on and either raises an error on an unseen category or, with `handle_unknown="ignore"`, encodes it as all zeros — either way, the output column layout stays identical to what training produced.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
cat_encoder = OneHotEncoder()
housing_cat_1hot = cat_encoder.fit_transform(housing_cat)
```

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Why can pd.get_dummies() silently produce a different set of columns in production than OneHotEncoder would?

blocks.content:
Most ML algorithms perform badly when input attributes sit on very different scales — here, room counts range up into the tens of thousands while median income tops out around 15, and without correction a model can end up effectively ignoring income and fixating on room counts purely because of their larger raw magnitude.

There are two standard fixes. **Min-max scaling** (often called normalization) rescales every value into a fixed range, typically 0 to 1, by subtracting the minimum and dividing by the range; `MinMaxScaler` does this and lets you pick a different target range via `feature_range`. **Standardization** instead subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, so the result has zero mean and unit variance, but — unlike min-max scaling — it does not confine values to a fixed range. That turns out to be an advantage with outliers: a single wildly wrong value can crush min-max-scaled data into a tiny sliver of its range, while standardization barely notices it. `StandardScaler` implements this, and crucially, scalers must only ever be *fit* on the training data — the already-learned scaling is then just *applied* to validation, test, and future data, never refit on them.

Scaling alone isn't enough for heavy-tailed distributions (where extreme values aren't exponentially rare), since both scaling methods will squash most values into a narrow band in that case. The fix is to reshape the distribution first — a square root or logarithm for a right-skewed positive attribute — or, for a distribution with multiple distinct peaks, to bucketize it into ranges, or add features measuring similarity to each peak using a radial basis function.

blocks.title: Worked out: one outlier under min-max scaling
blocks.content: Min-max scaling turns each value x into (x − min) / (max − min): subtract the minimum, then divide by the difference between the maximum and the minimum. In the book's example, median incomes usually range from 0 to 15, but one district has a median income of 100 by mistake. That outlier becomes the maximum, so it maps to (100 − 0) / (100 − 0) = 1, while a genuine top income of 15 maps to (15 − 0) / (100 − 0) = 0.15. All the real incomes are crushed into the range 0 to 0.15. Standardization instead subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation; it does not restrict values to a fixed range, and the book says it would not be much affected by the outlier.

blocks.content:
Scikit-Learn's built-in transformers cover a lot, but real projects always need something bespoke — a custom cleanup rule, or a way to combine specific columns. For a stateless transformation (nothing needs to be learned from data), `FunctionTransformer` wraps a plain function as a transformer with almost no ceremony — for example, wrapping `np.log` turns it into a proper transformer, and passing an `inverse_func` lets that transformation later be undone (useful when the *target*, not just the inputs, gets transformed).

When a transformer genuinely needs to learn something during `fit()` and reuse it in `transform()`, a full custom class is needed. Scikit-Learn relies on duck typing here — there's no required base class, only three expected methods: `fit()` (which must return `self`), `transform()`, and `fit_transform()`. Inheriting from `TransformerMixin` gives `fit_transform()` for free, and inheriting from `BaseEstimator` (while avoiding `*args`/`**kwargs` in the constructor) adds `get_params()`/`set_params()`, which hyperparameter search tools rely on.

A custom transformer can also lean on other estimators internally. The `ClusterSimilarity` class below does exactly that: its `fit()` runs k-means to locate cluster centers in the training data (weighted, here, by median house value, so pricier districts pull cluster centers toward them), and its `transform()` measures each row's Gaussian RBF similarity to every cluster center it found — turning raw geographic coordinates into a richer set of "how close is this district to each price hotspot" features that a model may find more useful than raw latitude and longitude alone.

items.term: Chaining It All Together with Pipelines

blocks.content:
With several transformation steps that must run in a specific order (impute, then scale, for instance), `Pipeline` chains them into a single object. Its constructor takes a list of (name, estimator) pairs; every step except the last must be a transformer, and the last can be anything — transformer or predictor. Calling `fit()` on the pipeline runs `fit_transform()` on every step in sequence, feeding each step's output into the next, and finishes by just calling `fit()` on the last one. If you don't care about naming steps yourself, `make_pipeline()` auto-generates names from each class name.

Since numeric and categorical columns need entirely different treatment, `ColumnTransformer` applies a different pipeline to a different subset of columns and concatenates the results side by side. Its constructor takes a list of (name, transformer, column-list) triples, and `make_column_selector()` can pick columns by dtype automatically instead of naming them by hand — handy since hardcoding a long column list is brittle.

The full preprocessing pipeline below is the payoff of everything explored so far: it computes the bedroom/room, room/household, and population/household ratios via a small reusable `ratio_pipeline()` helper, log-transforms the heavy-tailed count columns, adds the ten cluster-similarity features from the custom transformer, one-hot encodes the categorical column, and standardizes whatever's left over (just the housing age) through the `remainder` argument — one single object that turns a raw DataFrame into a fully prepared, 24-column NumPy array ready for a model, all with one `fit_transform()` call.

blocks.title: Worked out: where the 24 columns come from
blocks.content: The book lists the output names with `preprocessing.get_feature_names_out()`, and they add up as follows. The three ratio pipelines give 3 columns: `bedrooms__ratio`, `rooms_per_house__ratio` and `people_per_house__ratio`. The log pipeline gives 5 columns, one each for total_bedrooms, total_rooms, population, households and median_income. The `ClusterSimilarity` step, built with `n_clusters=10`, gives 10 cluster-similarity columns. The one-hot encoder gives 5 columns, one per ocean-proximity category (`<1H OCEAN`, `INLAND`, `ISLAND`, `NEAR BAY`, `NEAR OCEAN`). The remainder pipeline gives 1 column for housing_median_age. In total, 3 + 5 + 10 + 5 + 1 = 24, and the shape of the result is (16512, 24): one row per training district and one column per feature.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
def column_ratio(X):
    return X[:, [0]] / X[:, [1]]

def ratio_name(function_transformer, feature_names_in):
    return ["ratio"] # feature names out

def ratio_pipeline():
    return make_pipeline(
        SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
        FunctionTransformer(column_ratio, feature_names_out=ratio_name),
        StandardScaler())

log_pipeline = make_pipeline(
    SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
    FunctionTransformer(np.log, feature_names_out="one-to-one"),
    StandardScaler())
cluster_simil = ClusterSimilarity(n_clusters=10, gamma=1., random_state=42)
default_num_pipeline = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
                                     StandardScaler())
preprocessing = ColumnTransformer([
        ("bedrooms", ratio_pipeline(), ["total_bedrooms", "total_rooms"]),
        ("rooms_per_house", ratio_pipeline(), ["total_rooms", "households"]),
        ("people_per_house", ratio_pipeline(), ["population", "households"]),
        ("log", log_pipeline, ["total_bedrooms", "total_rooms", "population",
                               "households", "median_income"]),
        ("geo", cluster_simil, ["latitude", "longitude"]),
        ("cat", cat_pipeline, make_column_selector(dtype_include=object)),
    ],
    remainder=default_num_pipeline) # one column remaining: housing_median_age
```

items: In a Pipeline's list of (name, estimator) steps, which steps must be transformers and which one is exempt from that rule?

items.term: First Models: Underfitting and Overfitting in Action

blocks.content:
With preprocessing wrapped into one pipeline, trying a model is now almost trivial: chain the preprocessing pipeline with `LinearRegression` and call `fit()`. The resulting model's predictions on the training data are visibly imperfect — one prediction is off by over $200,000, two are off by about 25%, and two are off by less than 10% — and measuring RMSE on the training set confirms it numerically, at roughly $68,600. Since typical house values in this data run from about $120,000 to $265,000, an average error near $68,600 is a poor result, and it's a textbook case of **underfitting**: the model's predictions aren't accurate even on the data it was trained on, which points either to insufficiently informative features or an underpowered model — and since this model wasn't regularized, an overly-constrained model isn't the explanation here.

Swapping in a `DecisionTreeRegressor` — a substantially more flexible model capable of capturing complex nonlinear patterns — and repeating the same fit-and-measure routine produces a training RMSE of exactly 0.0. That is not a triumph; a model with zero error on the data it was trained on almost certainly memorized that data rather than learning a generalizable pattern, which is the signature of severe **overfitting**. The catch is that training-set error alone cannot distinguish a genuinely excellent model from one that has simply memorized its training examples — which is precisely why the next step is proper held-out evaluation rather than trusting the training score.

blocks.title: Worked out: the first five predictions
blocks.content: The book compares the linear model's first five training predictions, rounded to the nearest hundred, with the true labels. The predictions are 243,700, 372,400, 128,800, 94,400 and 328,300; the labels are 458,300, 483,800, 101,700, 96,100 and 361,800. The first prediction misses by 458,300 − 243,700 = 214,600, which is over 200,000. The second misses by 483,800 − 372,400 = 111,400, about 23% of its label, and the third by 128,800 − 101,700 = 27,100, about 27% of its label, so both are off by roughly 25%. The fourth misses by 1,700 (under 2%) and the fifth by 33,500 (about 9%), so both are off by less than 10%.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

tree_reg = make_pipeline(preprocessing, DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=42))
tree_reg.fit(housing, housing_labels)
```

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: A model scores a training RMSE of exactly 0.0. Should that be read as success? Why or why not?

blocks.content:
The decision tree's perfect training score is meaningless without touching the untouched test set, but the test set is off-limits until the very end — so a way is needed to estimate generalization performance using only the training data. **K-fold cross-validation** does this: split the training set into k non-overlapping chunks called folds (10 in this example), then repeat a train-and-evaluate cycle k times, each time holding out a different fold for evaluation and training on the remaining k−1 folds. The payoff is k separate performance scores instead of one.

Running this on the decision tree produces a very different picture than the earlier 0.0: a mean RMSE around $66,868 with a standard deviation around $2,061 — in other words, once evaluated on data it wasn't trained on, the tree performs barely better than plain linear regression (whose cross-validated mean RMSE is around $69,858), which confirms the earlier suspicion of overfitting. Having ten separate scores also delivers something a single train/validation split can't: a sense of how *precise* the estimate itself is, via that standard deviation — the tradeoff being that cross-validation costs roughly k times the compute of a single fit, since the model is trained from scratch on every fold.

A third model, `RandomForestRegressor` — which trains many decision trees on random data subsets and averages their outputs, a strategy the book calls an ensemble — comes out clearly ahead with a mean cross-validated RMSE around $47,020, though its own training-set RMSE (much lower still) shows some overfitting remains even here.

blocks.title: Why the cross-validation scores come out negative
blocks.content: Scikit-Learn's cross-validation features expect a utility function, where greater is better, rather than a cost function such as the RMSE, where lower is better. The scoring option `neg_root_mean_squared_error` therefore returns the opposite of each fold's RMSE, which is a negative number, and the minus sign in front of `cross_val_score(...)` switches it back to a positive RMSE. Calling `pd.Series(tree_rmses).describe()` on the 10 decision-tree scores gives a mean of 66,868.03 and a standard deviation of 2,060.97, which the book rounds to about 66,868 and 2,061. The same summary for the random forest gives a mean of 47,019.56 and a standard deviation of 1,033.96. For the linear model, the book reports a mean RMSE of 69,858 and a standard deviation of 4,182.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

tree_rmses = -cross_val_score(tree_reg, housing, housing_labels,
                              scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error", cv=10)
```

items: Scikit-Learn's cross_val_score with scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error" returns negative numbers. What do you have to do with them to get the actual RMSE, and why is the scoring function negative in the first place?

items.term: Fine-Tuning with Grid Search and Randomized Search

blocks.content:
Hand-tweaking hyperparameters one at a time is slow and easy to do badly, so `GridSearchCV` automates it: give it a dictionary (or list of dictionaries) naming which hyperparameters to try and which values for each, and it cross-validates every combination, keeping track of scores along the way. Because the preprocessing steps and the model both live inside one combined pipeline, the search can tune preprocessing hyperparameters (like the number of clusters in the custom `ClusterSimilarity` transformer) at the same time as model hyperparameters — addressed by a double-underscore path like `preprocessing__geo__n_clusters` that names the step and then the parameter within it. This matters because these hyperparameters can genuinely interact: the right number of clusters may depend on how many features the forest is allowed to consider per split, and vice versa. After the search finishes, `best_params_` names the winning combination and `best_estimator_` gives the refitted best pipeline; by default the winning combination is automatically retrained on the *entire* training set, since more data generally helps.

Grid search's weakness is that it must exhaustively try every listed combination, which becomes impractical fast as the search space grows. `RandomizedSearchCV` instead samples a fixed, chosen number of random combinations from given value ranges or probability distributions — so adding an unimportant hyperparameter to the search costs nothing extra (it just gets sampled a few times), unlike grid search, where it multiplies the total combinations. Scikit-Learn also offers halving variants of both searches, which spend limited resources on many candidates in an early round and progressively hand more resources only to the survivors of each round.

blocks.title: Worked out: counting grid-search combinations
blocks.content: Grid search multiplies the number of values listed for each hyperparameter. The book's first dictionary lists 3 values for `n_clusters` and 3 for `max_features`, which gives 3 × 3 = 9 combinations; the second lists 2 and 3 values, which gives 2 × 3 = 6. In total the search explores 9 + 6 = 15 combinations, and with 3-fold cross-validation each one is trained 3 times, for 15 × 3 = 45 rounds of training. The same rule explains the book's larger example: 6 hyperparameters with 10 possible values each give 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000,000 combinations, so grid search has no choice but to train the model a million times, whereas random search can run for any number of iterations you choose.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

full_pipeline = Pipeline([
    ("preprocessing", preprocessing),
    ("random_forest", RandomForestRegressor(random_state=42)),
])
param_grid = [
    {'preprocessing__geo__n_clusters': [5, 8, 10],
     'random_forest__max_features': [4, 6, 8]},
    {'preprocessing__geo__n_clusters': [10, 15],
     'random_forest__max_features': [6, 8, 10]},
]
grid_search = GridSearchCV(full_pipeline, param_grid, cv=3,
                           scoring='neg_root_mean_squared_error')
grid_search.fit(housing, housing_labels)
```

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: You have 6 hyperparameters to explore, each with 10 possible values. Why would RandomizedSearchCV usually be the more practical choice over GridSearchCV here?

items.term: Final Evaluation, Launch, and Ongoing Monitoring

blocks.content:
Before declaring victory, it's worth inspecting *why* the best model performs the way it does. A random forest exposes `feature_importances_`, a score per input feature showing how much it actually contributed to predictions — sorting these often reveals that a whole category of engineered feature barely matters (here, most of the one-hot-encoded ocean-proximity columns turn out close to useless, while median income and the engineered ratio features dominate), which is a legitimate reason to consider dropping the unhelpful ones.

Only once a model is genuinely considered finished does it ever touch the test set — one single evaluation, computing the final RMSE on data that has never influenced any decision up to this point. Because that RMSE is a single point estimate, it's good practice to also compute a confidence interval around it (using a t-distribution over the squared errors), so a stakeholder sees not just "41,424" but a plausible range around it — and critically, however that final number lands, you never go back and retune hyperparameters to chase a better test-set score, since doing so would just refit the model to the test set by another name and destroy the honesty of the estimate.

Getting the model into production is not the finish line either. A model needs monitoring for **model rot** (also called data drift) — slow, easy-to-miss performance decay as the real world diverges from what the model was trained on — sometimes inferred through downstream business metrics, sometimes through human review of samples. Sensible automation includes scheduled retraining on fresh data, automatically comparing a new candidate against the currently deployed model before replacing it, monitoring the *inputs* themselves for drift or new unseen categories, and keeping backups of every model and dataset version so a bad rollout can be reverted quickly.

blocks.title: Worked out: importance scores and the interval
blocks.content: Sorting the tuned random forest's `feature_importances_` puts `log__median_income` first at about 0.187, followed by `cat__ocean_proximity_INLAND` at about 0.075, `bedrooms__ratio` at about 0.069, `rooms_per_house__ratio` at about 0.054 and `people_per_house__ratio` at about 0.053. Median income scores more than twice as high as any other feature. At the bottom of the list sit `cat__ocean_proximity_NEAR BAY` at about 0.00015 and `cat__ocean_proximity_ISLAND` at about 0.00007, so the book concludes that only one ocean-proximity category is really useful and that you could try dropping the others. For the final test RMSE of 41,424, `scipy.stats.t.interval()` gives a 95% confidence interval from 39,275 to 43,467, with the point estimate roughly in the middle.

items.term: The MNIST Dataset and Scikit-Learn's Dataset Helpers

blocks.content:
This chapter switches from the regression problem of Chapter 2 to classification, and it does so using MNIST — a set of 70,000 grayscale images of handwritten digits, each 28x28 pixels. Because each pixel becomes one feature, every image is represented as a row of 784 numbers between 0 (white) and 255 (black), and each row's label is the digit it depicts, stored as a string like '5' rather than an integer.

Scikit-Learn's `sklearn.datasets` module groups its dataset helpers into three families: `fetch_*` functions download real datasets like MNIST from the internet, `load_*` functions ship small toy datasets bundled with the library itself, and `make_*` functions synthesize fake data for quick tests. Downloaded and loaded datasets typically arrive as a `Bunch` — a dictionary-like object exposing a description, the input matrix, and the target array as attributes.

`fetch_openml()` has one quirk worth remembering: it defaults to returning a Pandas DataFrame and Series, which is convenient for tabular data but awkward for image pixels, so passing `as_frame=False` gets you plain NumPy arrays instead. One more thing to notice before touching the data further: the MNIST split returned by Scikit-Learn is already divided into a 60,000-image training set and a 10,000-image test set, and the training portion is already shuffled — which matters because algorithms that are sensitive to instance ordering, and cross-validation folds that need a representative mix of digits, both depend on that shuffle having already happened.

blocks.title: Figure 3-1

items.term: Framing and Training a Binary Classifier

blocks.content:
To get started without tackling all ten digits at once, the chapter narrows the problem to a single binary decision: is this image a 5, or not? Building that '5-detector' starts with turning the multiclass label array into a boolean one — `y_train_5` is `True` wherever the original label is '5' and `False` everywhere else — so the classifier only ever has to answer yes or no.

For the model itself, the book reaches for `SGDClassifier`, built on stochastic gradient descent. The reasoning is practical rather than about raw accuracy: SGD updates its parameters using one training instance at a time instead of the whole dataset at once, which makes it efficient on very large datasets and, as a side effect, naturally suited to online learning (a topic from Chapter 1), where new instances can be incorporated as they arrive rather than requiring the whole training set to be reprocessed.

Once `sgd_clf.fit(X_train, y_train_5)` has run, `predict()` on a single reshaped instance returns a one-element boolean array. Getting a correct answer on one hand-picked digit feels satisfying, but it says nothing about how the model performs in general — which is exactly the gap the rest of the chapter exists to close.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
y_train_5 = (y_train == '5')   # True for all 5s, False for all other digits
y_test_5 = (y_test == '5')

from sklearn.linear_model import SGDClassifier

sgd_clf = SGDClassifier(random_state=42)
sgd_clf.fit(X_train, y_train_5)
```

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Why would framing '5 vs not-5' make this an easier first classifier to build than jumping straight to all ten digits?

items.term: Why Accuracy Lies: Cross-Validation on a Skewed Dataset

blocks.content:
The obvious way to score a classifier is cross-validated accuracy — the fraction of predictions that are correct — and running `cross_val_score` with three folds on the SGD 5-detector returns numbers above 95%. That looks outstanding until you build a deliberately useless baseline: `DummyClassifier`, which always predicts the single most frequent class regardless of the input. Because only around 10% of MNIST images are actually 5s, always guessing 'not a 5' is correct roughly 90% of the time — so the dummy classifier's cross-validated accuracy also comes in above 90%, despite never once detecting an actual 5.

That is the trap: on a skewed dataset, where one class vastly outnumbers the other, accuracy rewards a model for doing the easy, lazy thing. A 95%-accurate detector and a 90%-accurate detector that never fires are not nearly as far apart as the numbers suggest, and accuracy alone cannot tell them apart.

The chapter also shows how to hand-roll the same cross-validation loop using `StratifiedKFold`, which splits the data so each fold keeps a representative mix of the two classes, and `clone`, which produces an untrained copy of the classifier for each fold. Seeing the mechanics spelled out makes it clear that `cross_val_score` is doing nothing exotic — just repeated train/evaluate splits — which is useful once a project needs more control than the built-in function offers.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier

dummy_clf = DummyClassifier()
dummy_clf.fit(X_train, y_train_5)
print(any(dummy_clf.predict(X_train))) # prints False: no 5s detected
```

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Describe a real dataset you've worked with where accuracy alone would have been a misleading metric.

items.term: The Confusion Matrix, and Where Precision and Recall Come From

blocks.content:
Once accuracy has been shown to be misleading, the chapter reaches for a tool that shows the full picture: the confusion matrix. Its idea is simple — count how often instances that actually belong to class A get predicted as class B, for every pair of classes. Building one requires predictions that were never seen during training, so instead of touching the held-out test set early, the book uses `cross_val_predict`, which runs the same k-fold mechanics as `cross_val_score` but returns each instance's out-of-sample prediction rather than a score.

For the binary 5-detector, the resulting 2x2 matrix has a row for the actual negative (non-5) and actual positive (5) classes, and a column for each predicted class. Reading it names four outcomes: true negatives and false positives sit in the negative row, false negatives and true positives sit in the positive row — false positives are also called type I errors, and false negatives type II errors. A flawless classifier would have entries only along the diagonal, since every prediction would match the true class.

From these four counts come two of the chapter's central metrics. Precision is the fraction of positive predictions that were actually correct, and recall is the fraction of actual positives the classifier managed to catch. The chapter is careful to note that precision alone can be gamed — a classifier that makes exactly one very confident positive prediction, and gets it right, technically has 100% precision while being useless — which is why precision is always read alongside recall.

blocks.title: Worked out: reading the 5-detector's confusion matrix
blocks.content:
In `[[53892, 687], [1891, 3530]]`, the first row holds the actual non-5s: 53,892 were correctly classified as non-5s (true negatives) and 687 were wrongly classified as 5s (false positives). The second row holds the actual 5s: 1,891 were wrongly classified as non-5s (false negatives) and 3,530 were correctly classified as 5s (true positives).

Putting these counts into the two equations gives precision = 3,530 / (687 + 3,530) ≈ 0.837 and recall = 3,530 / (1,891 + 3,530) ≈ 0.651. A perfect classifier on the same 60,000 training images would give `[[54579, 0], [0, 5421]]`: all 53,892 + 687 = 54,579 non-5s and all 1,891 + 3,530 = 5,421 5s land on the main diagonal.

items.term: Precision, Recall and F1 in Practice

blocks.content:
With precision and recall defined, Scikit-Learn's `precision_score` and `recall_score` turn the confusion-matrix counts into the two headline numbers for the 5-detector: roughly 83.7% precision and 65.1% recall. Read plainly, that means whenever the classifier claims an image is a 5 it is right about 84% of the time, but it only manages to find about two-thirds of the 5s that actually exist in the data — a much less flattering picture than the 95%+ accuracy from earlier suggested.

Because juggling two numbers is awkward when comparing classifiers, the chapter introduces the F1 score, the harmonic mean of precision and recall rather than their ordinary average. The harmonic mean is the key design choice: it punishes a low value in either precision or recall far more severely than an arithmetic mean would, so a classifier only earns a high F1 score if both numbers are genuinely good — it cannot hide a weak recall behind a strong precision.

But a single balanced number is not always what a project needs. The book contrasts two real scenarios: a filter deciding whether videos are safe for children should lean toward high precision even at the cost of recall (better to reject some good videos than let one bad one through), while a system flagging shoplifters on camera should lean toward high recall even at low precision (a few false alarms are an acceptable price for catching almost every real case). Because pushing one of the two up reliably pushes the other down, this trade-off gets its own name and its own section next.

blocks.title: Equation 3-3
blocks.caption: F score

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, recall_score

precision_score(y_train_5, y_train_pred) # == 3530 / (687 + 3530)
recall_score(y_train_5, y_train_pred) # == 3530 / (1891 + 3530)

from sklearn.metrics import f1_score

f1_score(y_train_5, y_train_pred)
```

items.term: The Precision/Recall Trade-off and Choosing a Threshold

blocks.content:
The precision/recall trade-off has a concrete mechanism behind it: SGDClassifier assigns every instance a decision score, and compares that score to a threshold to decide positive or negative. Move the threshold up and fewer instances clear the bar, which typically raises precision (the ones that do clear it are more likely to be real positives) while lowering recall (some real positives now fall short); move it down and the effect reverses. Scikit-Learn does not expose a way to set this threshold directly through `predict()`, but `decision_function()` hands back the raw score for any instance, so you can compare it to whatever threshold you choose yourself.

To pick a threshold deliberately rather than by guesswork, the workflow is: get out-of-sample decision scores for every training instance via `cross_val_predict(..., method="decision_function")`, then feed those scores into `precision_recall_curve()`, which reports the precision and recall that would result at every possible threshold. From there, if you have a target precision in mind — say 90% — you can search the precision array for the first threshold that clears it using `argmax()` on a boolean condition, since `argmax` conveniently returns the index of the first `True` value.

The catch the chapter is careful to flag: hitting a chosen precision is easy — just raise the threshold far enough — but the resulting recall might be unacceptably low (48% in the book's example). A precision number quoted alone is close to meaningless; the recall at that same threshold is what tells you whether the trade-off is actually livable for your use case.

blocks.title: Worked out: how the threshold changes the numbers
blocks.content:
In Figure 3-4 the digits are ranked by score. With the threshold at the central arrow, 4 true positives (actual 5s) and 1 false positive (a 6) sit to its right, so precision is 4 out of 5, or 80%. Of the 6 actual 5s, 4 are detected, so recall is 4 out of 6, or 67%. Moving the threshold to the right arrow turns the 6 into a true negative and one 5 into a false negative: precision rises to 100% and recall drops to 50%. Precision can dip on the way, though: one digit to the right of the central arrow it goes from 4/5 (80%) down to 3/4 (75%).

`SGDClassifier` uses a threshold of 0. The example digit scores about 2,164, so it is called a 5, but with a threshold of 3,000 it is missed. The lowest threshold giving at least 90% precision is about 3,370, where precision is 90.0% and recall only 48.0%.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
y_scores = cross_val_predict(sgd_clf, X_train, y_train_5, cv=3,
                             method="decision_function")

from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve

precisions, recalls, thresholds = precision_recall_curve(y_train_5, y_scores)

idx_for_90_precision = (precisions >= 0.90).argmax()
threshold_for_90_precision = thresholds[idx_for_90_precision]
threshold_for_90_precision
```

items: If someone tells you their model hits 95% precision, what single follow-up question should you ask, and why?

blocks.content:
The ROC curve is the precision/recall curve's close cousin, built from a different pair of rates. Instead of precision, it plots the true positive rate (which is just recall under another name) against the false positive rate — the fraction of actual negatives that get wrongly flagged as positive. The false positive rate is also 1 minus the true negative rate, where the true negative rate (the fraction of actual negatives correctly left alone) goes by the name specificity — so the ROC curve is really sensitivity plotted against 1 minus specificity.

`roc_curve()` computes matching false-positive-rate and true-positive-rate pairs across every threshold, in the same spirit as `precision_recall_curve()`. Plotted, a genuinely useful classifier's curve bows up and to the left, away from the diagonal line that represents a classifier making pure random guesses. Collapsing the whole curve into a single number gives the area under the curve (AUC): 1.0 for a perfect classifier, 0.5 for a random one, computed directly with `roc_auc_score()`.

The chapter's rule of thumb for choosing between the two curve types matters more than it might first appear: prefer the precision/recall curve when the positive class is rare, or when false positives matter more than false negatives; otherwise the ROC curve is fine. The reason is concrete here — with 5s being a small minority of MNIST, the ROC AUC can look impressively close to 1 even though the PR curve, plotted over the same data, makes clear there is real room left to improve.

blocks.title: Worked out: the 5-detector's ROC numbers
blocks.content:
For the SGD 5-detector's cross-validated scores, `roc_auc_score(y_train_5, y_scores)` returns about 0.9605, close to the 1.0 of a perfect classifier. On the ROC curve, the threshold chosen for 90% precision sits at 48% recall, and the curve shows the same kind of trade-off as before: the higher the recall (TPR), the more false positives (FPR) the classifier produces.

The high AUC is mostly because there are few positives (5s) compared with the negatives (non-5s). The precision/recall curve for the same scores tells a different story: it could really be closer to the top-right corner, so the classifier still has room for improvement.

blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve

fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y_train_5, y_scores)

from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

roc_auc_score(y_train_5, y_scores)
```

items.term: Comparing Classifiers: Random Forest vs SGD

blocks.content:
To see whether the SGD 5-detector can be beaten, the chapter brings in `RandomForestClassifier` and compares its precision/recall behavior directly. The comparison hits one snag immediately: `RandomForestClassifier` has no `decision_function()` method, so instead of a raw score you use `predict_proba()`, which returns an estimated probability for each class. Since the two classes' probabilities always sum to 100%, the probability assigned to the positive class works as a perfectly good substitute score for building a precision/recall curve — obtained the same way as before, via `cross_val_predict(..., method="predict_proba")`.

Before trusting those numbers too far, the book adds an important caveat: these are estimated probabilities, not verified ones. Looking at every instance the model called positive with 50-60% estimated confidence, roughly 94% of them turned out to actually be positive — meaning the model was, in that band, considerably more accurate than its own stated confidence implied. Scikit-Learn's calibration tools exist specifically to correct this kind of mismatch between estimated and real probabilities.

Plotting the random forest's PR curve alongside the SGD classifier's makes the difference visible at a glance: the forest's curve sits much closer to the ideal top-right corner across the board, and its F1 score and ROC AUC both come out clearly higher. This is the payoff of building reusable evaluation tooling in the first half of the chapter — once PR curves, F1, and ROC AUC are working for one classifier, comparing a second one is nearly free.

blocks.title: Worked out: the forest's probabilities and scores
blocks.content:
For the first two training images, `y_probas_forest[:2]` returns `[[0.11, 0.89], [0.99, 0.01]]`. The model says the first image is positive with 89% probability and the second is negative with 99% probability, and each row adds up to 100%. The second column holds the positive-class probabilities, so `y_probas_forest[:, 1]` is the score given to `precision_recall_curve()`.

Calling an image a 5 when that probability is at least 50% gives the forest an F1 score of about 0.9242, against about 0.7325 for the SGD 5-detector, with about 99.1% precision and 86.6% recall. Computed from the probabilities themselves, the forest's ROC AUC is about 0.9983, against about 0.9605 for SGD.

blocks.content:

```python
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

forest_clf = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)

y_probas_forest = cross_val_predict(forest_clf, X_train, y_train_5, cv=3,
                                    method="predict_proba")
```

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Why is it fair to use predict_proba()'s positive-class probability as a substitute for decision_function() when building a PR curve?

blocks.content:
Digit recognition is really a ten-class problem, and getting there from binary classifiers takes one of two strategies. One-versus-the-rest (OvR) trains one binary classifier per class — a 0-detector, a 1-detector, and so on — and classifies a new instance by running it through all of them and keeping whichever classifier reported the highest confidence score. One-versus-one (OvO) instead trains a separate classifier for every pair of classes; for 10 digits that means 45 classifiers, and a new instance is classified by having every pair 'vote' and counting which class wins the most duels.

OvO's real advantage shows up for algorithms that scale poorly as the training set grows, such as support vector machines: training 45 classifiers, each only on the two classes it needs to tell apart, ends up cheaper than training a smaller number of classifiers on the full dataset. For most other algorithms, OvR is the default. Scikit-Learn detects when a naturally-binary classifier is handed a multiclass target and picks OvO or OvR automatically, though `OneVsOneClassifier` and `OneVsRestClassifier` exist to force one strategy explicitly.

Two practical details round this out. `classes_` stores the trained classifier's class labels in order, which is needed to translate a raw index (from `argmax()` on the decision scores) back into an actual digit label. And simply standardizing the pixel values before training — nothing about the model itself — lifted SGDClassifier's cross-validated accuracy from around 86% to around 90%, a reminder that scaling is not just a Chapter 2 regression trick.

blocks.title: Worked out: counting classifiers and reading the scores
blocks.content:
With N classes, OvO trains one classifier per pair of classes, which is N × (N – 1) / 2. For the 10 digits that is 10 × 9 / 2 = 45 classifiers. OvR trains one classifier per class, so 10, and `len(ovr_clf.estimators_)` indeed returns 10.

For the example digit, the SVC (which used OvO) returns 10 scores from `decision_function()`, one per class. Each score is the number of duels that class won, plus or minus a small tweak of at most 0.33 to break ties. The highest score is 9.3, at index 5, and `svm_clf.classes_[5]` is '5'.

For the ten-digit `SGDClassifier`, the three cross-validation folds scored 0.87365, 0.85835 and 0.8689 accuracy. After scaling the inputs with `StandardScaler`, the folds scored 0.8983, 0.891 and 0.9018.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
from sklearn.svm import SVC

svm_clf = SVC(random_state=42)
svm_clf.fit(X_train[:2000], y_train[:2000]) # y_train, not y_train_5
```

items.term: Error Analysis With the Confusion Matrix

blocks.content:
With a promising model in hand, the natural next step is to study exactly how it fails, and the confusion matrix is the tool for that too — just extended from 2x2 to 10x10. Scikit-Learn's `ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions()` turns that grid into a picture where a strong diagonal signals mostly-correct predictions at a glance, but raw counts alone can mislead: a darker cell for the digit 5 might mean more errors on 5s, or it might just mean there are fewer 5s in the dataset to begin with.

Setting `normalize="true"` fixes that by dividing every cell by its row's total, so every row reads as a percentage of that true class rather than a raw count — comparable across digits regardless of how many examples of each exist. That normalized view shows only about 82% of 5s were classified correctly, with the most common mistake being 8 — 10% of all 5s were called 8s, while only 2% of 8s were called 5s, a clear reminder that confusion matrices are not symmetric.

To make faint-but-real error patterns visible, the book also zeroes out every correct prediction with a `sample_weight` before normalizing, and can normalize by predicted column instead of true row (`normalize="pred"`) to ask the complementary question. One care point matters here: a normalized error percentage describes a slice of the errors, not the whole class — 36% in the row-7/column-9 cell means 36% of the mistakes made on 7s were called 9, not that 36% of all 7s were. Reading that difference correctly is what turns this analysis into concrete next steps, like gathering more training data resembling the true source of confusion or engineering features (such as counting closed loops) that separate the confused digits.

blocks.title: Worked out: the percentages in the error plots
blocks.content:
The errors-only plot passes `sample_weight = (y_train_pred != y_train)`, which puts zero weight on every correct prediction, so only the errors are left when each row is normalized. That is why the 36% at row 7, column 9 is a share of the errors made on 7s. Out of all 7s, only 3% were misclassified as 9s, as the full row-normalized plot (Figure 3-9, right) shows.

With `normalize="pred"`, each column is divided by its own total instead. For example, 56% of the images wrongly classified as 7s are actually 9s. In the errors-only plot, the column for class 8 is really bright: many digits get misclassified as 8s, which is why the chapter suggests spending effort on reducing the false 8s.

blocks.content:
Not every classification problem has exactly one right answer per instance. A face-recognition system shown a photo of two specific people should tag both of them, not force a single label — that is multilabel classification, where the output is a set of independent binary tags rather than one class choice. The chapter's toy version tags each MNIST digit with two labels at once: whether it is 'large' (7, 8, or 9) and whether it is odd, combined into a two-column array and fed to `KNeighborsClassifier`, which is one of the classifiers that actually supports multilabel targets natively.

Scoring a multilabel classifier means picking a way to combine per-label scores into one number, and the choice matters. Averaging each label's F1 score with `average="macro"` treats every label as equally important; `average="weighted"` instead weights each label's contribution by its support — how many instances actually carry that label — which is the more honest choice when the labels are not evenly represented in the data.

Classifiers that cannot handle multilabel targets natively, like SVC, can still be pressed into service by training one independent binary model per label — but that throws away any relationship between the labels, such as the fact that large digits are twice as likely to be odd as even. `ClassifierChain` fixes this by feeding each model in the chain not just the input features but also the predictions from every model earlier in the chain, optionally trained on cross-validated out-of-sample predictions so the chain does not simply memorize the true labels.

blocks.title: The Alice, Bob and Charlie example
blocks.content:
The chapter's face-recognition example uses a classifier trained to recognize three faces: Alice, Bob and Charlie. It outputs one True/False tag per person, in that order. Shown a picture of Alice and Charlie, it should output `[True, False, True]`, meaning "Alice yes, Bob no, Charlie yes".

The digit version works the same way with two tags, large (7, 8 or 9) first and odd second. For the example digit, a 5, `knn_clf.predict([some_digit])` returns `[[False, True]]`, because a 5 is not large but is odd. Among the large digits, 7 and 9 are odd and only 8 is even, which is why a large digit is twice as likely to be odd as even.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

y_train_large = (y_train >= '7')
y_train_odd = (y_train.astype('int8') % 2 == 1)
y_multilabel = np.c_[y_train_large, y_train_odd]

knn_clf = KNeighborsClassifier()
knn_clf.fit(X_train, y_multilabel)
```

blocks.title: Book exercise
items: Explain why ClassifierChain can capture label dependencies that training one independent model per label cannot.

blocks.content:
The final generalization in the chapter is multioutput classification, and it is best understood through a concrete example rather than a definition: an image-denoising system. Feed the model a noisy digit image, built by adding random pixel-level noise to real MNIST images, and ask it to predict the original clean image back — one label per pixel, and each of those 784 labels can take any value from 0 to 255, not just true or false. That is what makes it multioutput rather than plain multilabel: multilabel assumes each label is binary, and here each 'label' is really its own miniature multiclass (or, arguably, regression) problem.

The book is candid that this blurs the line between classification and regression — predicting a pixel's intensity looks a lot more like regression than like picking a class — and notes multioutput systems in general are not restricted to classification tasks at all; a system could just as easily mix class labels and numeric labels together.

Mechanically nothing new is required: the same `KNeighborsClassifier` used for the earlier multilabel example is trained here on noisy inputs paired with their original clean versions as targets, and calling `predict()` on a noisy test image returns a full reconstructed image rather than a single tag. The result closes out the chapter's tour by showing that the classification toolbox — from picking metrics to comparing models — scales to problems that do not look like classification at first glance.

```python
np.random.seed(42) # to make this code example reproducible
noise = np.random.randint(0, 100, (len(X_train), 784))
X_train_mod = X_train + noise
```

blocks.title: 4 book exercises
items: Exercise 1: Try to build a classifier for the MNIST dataset that achieves over 97% accuracy on the test set. Hint: the KNeighborsClassifier works quite well for this task; you just need to find good hyperparameter values (try a grid search on the weights and n_neighbors hyperparameters).

Exercise 2: Write a function that can shift an MNIST image in any direction (left, right, up, or down) by one pixel. Then, for each image in the training set, create four shifted copies (one per direction) and add them to the training set. Finally, train your best model on this expanded training set and measure its accuracy on the test set. You should observe that your model performs even better now! This technique of artificially growing the training set is called data augmentation or training set expansion.

Exercise 3: Tackle the Titanic dataset. A great place to start is on Kaggle. Alternatively, you can download the data from https://homl.info/titanic.tgz and unzip this tarball like you did for the housing data in Chapter 2. This will give you two CSV files, train.csv and test.csv, which you can load using pandas.read_csv(). The goal is to train a classifier that can predict the Survived column based on the other columns.

Exercise 4: Build a spam classifier (a more challenging exercise):
a. Download examples of spam and ham from Apache SpamAssassin's public datasets.
b. Unzip the datasets and familiarize yourself with the data format.
c. Split the data into a training set and a test set.
d. Write a data preparation pipeline to convert each email into a feature vector. Your preparation pipeline should transform an email into a (sparse) vector that indicates the presence or absence of each possible word. For example, if all emails only ever contain four words, "Hello", "how", "are", "you", then the email "Hello you Hello Hello you" would be converted into a vector [1, 0, 0, 1] (meaning ["Hello" is present, "how" is absent, "are" is absent, "you" is present]), or [3, 0, 0, 2] if you prefer to count the number of occurrences of each word. You may want to add hyperparameters to your preparation pipeline to control whether or not to strip off email headers, convert each email to lowercase, remove punctuation, replace all URLs with "URL", replace all numbers with "NUMBER", or even perform stemming (i.e., trim off word endings; there are Python libraries available to do this).
e. Finally, try out several classifiers and see if you can build a great spam classifier, with both high recall and high precision.

blocks.content:
A linear regression model makes a prediction the same way you'd guess a house price from a checklist: take each input number, multiply it by a weight that says how much that input matters, add the results together, then add one more constant that shifts the whole result up or down. That constant is the bias term (also called the intercept) — it's the prediction the model would make if every feature were zero. Change one weight and every prediction shifts along that one feature's direction; change the bias and every prediction shifts by the same flat amount no matter what the inputs are.

Written out with n features, the prediction ŷ is θ0 (the bias) plus θ1x1 plus θ2x2, and so on through θnxn. That is a lot of terms to write for every single prediction, so the chapter switches to a compact vector notation: pack the weights (bias out front) into one vector θ, pack the feature values (with a fixed 1 slotted in for the bias) into another vector x, and the whole weighted sum collapses into one dot product, θ·x. Nothing about the model changed — it is still the same weighted sum — only the notation got shorter. This dot-product view is what the rest of the chapter reuses everywhere: training a linear model always means searching for the vector θ that makes θ·x land as close as possible to the true target y across every training example.

items.term: Training by Formula: The Normal Equation

blocks.content:
Training a linear regression model means finding the θ vector that makes predictions land as close as possible to the true targets, and "as close as possible" is measured by the mean squared error (MSE): average the squared gap between each prediction and its true value, so a few big misses hurt the score far more than many tiny ones. For plain linear regression there is a shortcut: instead of searching for the best θ by trial and error, one formula — the Normal equation — computes it directly from the data in a single step.

Running it on a small synthetic dataset (y = 4 + 3x plus random noise) makes the abstraction concrete. Generate 100 points from that rule, plug the feature matrix and the targets into the formula, and the result comes out close to but not exactly [4, 3] — something like [4.215, 2.770]. That gap is entirely the noise: with perfectly clean data the equation would recover [4, 3] exactly, and the smaller or noisier the dataset, the further the estimate tends to drift.

Scikit-Learn's LinearRegression class does not actually run this literal matrix-inversion formula under the hood — it uses a matrix factorization technique (SVD) that computes a pseudoinverse instead. That route is more efficient and, unlike the raw Normal equation, it never breaks: the Normal equation can fail outright when X-transpose-X is not invertible (which happens with more features than instances, or duplicated features), while the pseudoinverse is always defined. Both approaches share one limitation: inverting a matrix that grows with the number of features gets expensive fast — doubling the feature count roughly multiplies the compute time by 5 to 8 times for the raw inversion, and by about 4 times even for the faster SVD route. Neither approach cares much about the number of training instances, so both stay fast on huge datasets as long as the data fits in memory.

blocks.title: Worked out: where the 5.3-to-8 and 4 times figures come from
blocks.content:
The Normal equation inverts XᵀX, which is an (n + 1) × (n + 1) matrix, where n is the number of features. Inverting a matrix of that size typically costs about $O(n^{2.4})$ to $O(n^3)$, depending on the implementation. Doubling n therefore multiplies the computation time by roughly $2^{2.4} = 5.3$ up to $2^3 = 8$. The SVD approach used by Scikit-Learn's `LinearRegression` class is about $O(n^2)$, so doubling the features multiplies the time by roughly $2^2 = 4$.

The number of instances behaves differently: both approaches are linear in it, $O(m)$, so twice as many instances take roughly twice as long. That is why they handle large training sets efficiently, provided the data fits in memory, yet both get very slow when the number of features grows large, for example 100,000.

```python
import numpy as np
```

items.term: Gradient Descent: Feeling Your Way to the Minimum

blocks.content:
The Normal equation only works for linear regression's exact MSE formula, and it gets expensive as the number of features grows. Gradient descent is a general-purpose alternative: instead of solving for the best θ in one step, it starts from a random guess and nudges θ a little at a time, always moving in whichever direction most reduces the cost function right now — like feeling your way downhill in thick fog by sensing the slope under your feet.

The size of each step is set by a single hyperparameter, the learning rate. Make it too small and the algorithm needs an enormous number of tiny steps to reach the bottom, which is safe but slow. Make it too large and each step can overshoot the minimum and land higher up the opposite side of the valley than where it started — repeat that a few times and the algorithm diverges, wandering farther from a solution rather than closer.

Two extra facts make gradient descent tractable for linear regression specifically. First, the MSE cost function is convex — picture one smooth bowl with no dips or ridges — so there is exactly one minimum to find, and gradient descent is guaranteed to reach it eventually as long as the learning rate is sane. Second, the bowl's shape depends on how the features are scaled: if one feature's values are far larger than another's, the bowl becomes a long narrow trench, and descent crawls sideways before finding the way down. Scaling every feature to a similar range (with something like StandardScaler) turns that trench back into a round bowl and speeds up convergence dramatically.

items.term: Batch Gradient Descent: One Step, the Whole Training Set

blocks.content:
To actually move θ downhill you need to know which direction is downhill, and that means computing the partial derivative of the cost function with respect to every parameter — how much the MSE would change if you nudged that one weight slightly. Stack all of those partial derivatives together and you get the gradient vector, which points uphill; step in the opposite direction and you are heading toward lower cost. Batch gradient descent computes that gradient using every single training instance at every step — hence "batch" — then updates all of θ at once: subtract the gradient vector, scaled by the learning rate η, from the current θ.

The code that implements this is short: initialize θ randomly, then repeat a fixed number of times (each full pass through the data is called an epoch): compute the gradient over the whole training set, then take one step of size η in the opposite direction. Run it for 1,000 epochs with η = 0.1 on the same noisy linear data used for the Normal equation, and θ converges to the exact same answer the Normal equation found — which makes sense, since both are hunting for the minimum of the same convex bowl.

The catch is cost: recomputing the gradient over the entire training set at every single step is why batch GD is painfully slow once the training set is large. It also cannot be updated on the fly as new data streams in — every step needs the whole dataset in hand. On the plus side, it scales far better with the number of features than the Normal equation does, so it is the better choice when there are hundreds of thousands of features.

blocks.title: Worked out: what the batch GD loop returns
blocks.content:
Each pass of the loop does two things. First it computes the whole gradient vector at once, `gradients = 2 / m * X_b.T @ (X_b @ theta - y)`, which is Equation 4-6 applied to all the training instances. Then it steps the other way, `theta = theta - eta * gradients`, with η = 0.1, which is Equation 4-7.

After 1,000 of these epochs, starting from random values, `theta` comes out as [[4.21509616], [2.77011339]]. The Normal equation's `theta_best` on the same data was also [[4.21509616], [2.77011339]], so the two methods agree on every printed digit. Because every step uses the whole batch of training data, the book remarks that full gradient descent would probably be a better name for the algorithm.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
eta = 0.1 # learning rate
n_epochs = 1000
m = len(X_b) # number of instances

np.random.seed(42)
theta = np.random.randn(2, 1) # randomly initialized model parameters

for epoch in range(n_epochs):
    gradients = 2 / m * X_b.T @ (X_b @ theta - y)
    theta = theta - eta * gradients
```

items.term: Stochastic Gradient Descent: One Random Instance at a Time

blocks.content:
Batch gradient descent's biggest weakness is needing the whole training set for every single step. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) fixes that by going to the opposite extreme: at each step it grabs one random training instance, computes the gradient from that single example alone, and takes a step based on just that. Each step is nearly free computationally, which makes SGD fast even on datasets too big to fit in memory, since only one instance needs to be loaded at a time.

The cost of that speed is noise: instead of gliding smoothly toward the minimum, the cost bounces around erratically, decreasing only on average. It ends up near the minimum but keeps jittering around it forever rather than settling. That randomness has one silver lining — an irregular cost surface with bumps and local minima is much easier for SGD to escape than for batch GD, since a wild step can leap right out of a shallow dip.

The standard fix for the settling problem is a learning schedule: start with large steps (which helps escape bad local spots early) and shrink the learning rate as training goes on, so steps get smaller and the final position lands closer to the true minimum instead of jittering around it. The demo code runs only 50 epochs (versus batch GD's 1,000) and still lands close to the Normal equation's answer. One requirement that is easy to violate accidentally: the instances fed to SGD need to look independent and identically distributed over the run, which is usually guaranteed simply by shuffling — feed it data sorted by label instead, and SGD will fixate on optimizing for one label at a time and never settle near the true optimum. Scikit-Learn's SGDRegressor does the same job: it defaults to optimizing the MSE cost function and uses its own default learning schedule (different from the demo's), while the book's example switches regularization off explicitly with penalty=None.

blocks.title: Worked out: how close SGD and SGDRegressor get
blocks.content:
The demo loop picks a random instance m times per epoch, so some instances may be picked several times in an epoch while others are not picked at all. After only 50 epochs it returns `theta` = [[4.21076011], [2.74856079]], against [[4.21509616], [2.77011339]] from the Normal equation: a good solution, but not the optimal one.

Scikit-Learn's `SGDRegressor(max_iter=1000, tol=1e-5, penalty=None, eta0=0.01, n_iter_no_change=100, random_state=42)` runs for at most 1,000 epochs, or until the loss drops by less than $10^{-5}$ during 100 epochs. It starts from a learning rate of 0.01 and uses its own default learning schedule. It finds an intercept of 4.21278812 and a weight of 2.77270267, again quite close to the solution of the Normal equation.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
n_epochs = 50
t0, t1 = 5, 50 # learning schedule hyperparameters

def learning_schedule(t):
    return t0 / (t + t1)

np.random.seed(42)
theta = np.random.randn(2, 1) # random initialization

for epoch in range(n_epochs):
    for iteration in range(m):
        random_index = np.random.randint(m)
        xi = X_b[random_index : random_index + 1]
        yi = y[random_index : random_index + 1]
        gradients = 2 * xi.T @ (xi @ theta - yi) # for SGD, do not divide by m
        eta = learning_schedule(epoch * m + iteration)
        theta = theta - eta * gradients
```

items.term: Mini-Batch Gradient Descent and Choosing Among the Three

blocks.content:
Mini-batch gradient descent sits between the other two: instead of using the whole training set (batch) or a single instance (stochastic) at each step, it computes the gradient over a small random subset — a mini-batch — of instances. This keeps each step reasonably cheap while giving hardware, especially GPUs, enough data per step to exploit fast matrix-multiplication routines, a speed advantage stochastic GD cannot get from working one row at a time.

In terms of behavior, mini-batch GD's path through parameter space is less erratic than pure stochastic GD — with a large enough mini-batch it walks a steadier line toward the minimum — but because it is still not using the full dataset at every step, it can end up wandering around the minimum rather than stopping exactly on it, the same trade-off stochastic GD has. Comparing all three algorithms against the closed-form options: the Normal equation and SVD only work for linear regression and are the only ones with zero hyperparameters to tune, but both get slow as the number of features grows large and neither supports learning from a streaming data source. The three gradient descent variants all scale to huge numbers of features, and (aside from plain batch GD) support learning from data too large to hold in memory all at once — the price is a learning rate to tune and, for stochastic and mini-batch, some residual noise around the final answer rather than a clean stop exactly at the minimum.

items.term: Polynomial Regression: Fitting Curves with a Straight-Line Model

blocks.content:
A straight line cannot fit curved data, but you do not need a fundamentally different algorithm to handle it — you can trick a linear model into fitting curves by handing it extra features. Take your one feature x, add x² (and x³, and so on) as additional columns, and train an ordinary linear regression on the expanded set. The model is still linear in its parameters; it is just being handed a nonlinear transformation of the original input. This is polynomial regression, and Scikit-Learn's PolynomialFeatures class does the transformation for you: give it degree=2 with one input feature, and every row grows a second column holding that feature's square.

Fit an ordinary LinearRegression on this expanded data, generated from a true quadratic relationship (y = 0.5x² + x + 2 plus noise), and the recovered coefficients land close to the real ones. With more than one original feature, PolynomialFeatures does something linear regression alone never could: it also generates every cross-combination up to the chosen degree — for two features a and b at degree 3, that is not just each feature's own square and cube, but also every mixed product between them — letting the model discover interactions between features. That power has a cost worth remembering: the number of features PolynomialFeatures produces grows combinatorially with the degree and the number of original features, so a large degree on many features can explode into an unmanageable number of columns fast.

blocks.title: Worked out: the fitted coefficients, and the feature count
blocks.content:
Fitting `LinearRegression` to `X_poly` (the feature and its square) gives `intercept_` = 1.78134581 and `coef_` = [0.93366893, 0.56456263]. The first weight belongs to x₁ and the second to x₁², so the model estimates ŷ = 0.56x₁² + 0.93x₁ + 1.78. The data came from y = 0.5x₁² + 1.0x₁ + 2.0 plus Gaussian noise, so each learned value lands close to the true one without matching it: 0.56 against 0.5, 0.93 against 1.0, and 1.78 against 2.0.

The growth in columns also has a formula: `PolynomialFeatures(degree=d)` turns an array of n features into (n + d)! / d!n! features, where n! = 1 × 2 × 3 × ⋯ × n. For two features a and b with degree=3, it adds a², a³, b² and b³, and also the combinations ab, a²b and ab².

items.term: Learning Curves and the Bias/Variance Trade-off

blocks.content:
Cross-validation tells you a model's overall generalization score, but learning curves show you how that score got there. A learning curve plots two lines — training error and validation error — as the model is trained on progressively larger slices of the training set. Their shapes diagnose the problem. For a plain linear model fit to curved data, the training error climbs to a plateau while the validation error slowly falls to one, and the two end up close together, but both plateau high: the model cannot do well even on the data it was trained on, because a straight line genuinely cannot represent the underlying curve. That pattern — both curves flat and both bad — is the signature of underfitting, and the fix is not more data (more data will not help a shape the model structurally cannot represent) but a better model or better features.

Now retrain a 10th-degree polynomial on the same data: the training error drops much lower, but a visible gap opens up between the training curve and the validation curve — the model does noticeably better on data it has already seen than on new data. That gap is the signature of overfitting, and it shrinks as more training data is added, because a model with too many degrees of freedom needs more examples before it can no longer just memorize idiosyncrasies of a small sample.

The theory behind this: a model's generalization error decomposes into three sources. Bias is error from wrong assumptions (fitting a line to curved data) — high bias means underfitting. Variance is error from the model being overly sensitive to the exact training sample it saw (a wiggly, many-parameter model) — high variance means overfitting. Irreducible error is baseline noise in the data itself that no model can remove; only cleaning the data helps that part. Making a model more complex trades bias for variance, so tuning model complexity is really tuning this trade-off, never eliminating both sides at once.

blocks.title: Why the curves move, and which way the trade-off goes
blocks.content:
With just one or two training instances, a model can fit them perfectly, so the training error starts at zero. As new instances are added, the noise and the curve in the data make a perfect fit impossible, and the training error rises to a plateau. The validation error does the opposite: a model trained on very few instances cannot generalize, so the error starts large and then slowly goes down to a plateau.

The trade-off has a fixed direction. Increasing a model's complexity typically increases its variance and reduces its bias; reducing its complexity increases its bias and reduces its variance. So an underfitting, high-bias model needs a better model or better features, and a simpler model would only add bias. An overfitting model can be improved by feeding it more training data until the validation error reaches the training error.

items.term: Ridge Regression: Keeping the Weights Small

blocks.content:
Regularization is the general fix for overfitting: constrain the model so it has less freedom to contort itself around the training data's noise. Ridge regression regularizes a linear model by adding a penalty term to the cost function equal to a scaled sum of the squared feature weights — so training is no longer just "fit the data as closely as possible" but "fit the data closely while also keeping the weights small." Crucially, the bias term θ0 is left out of the penalty; only the feature weights are pushed toward zero.

The strength of this pull is set by a hyperparameter, α (alpha). Set α = 0 and ridge regression is just ordinary linear regression — no constraint at all. Crank α up and the weights get squeezed closer and closer to zero, until at a very large α the model flattens into roughly a constant line through the data's average, regardless of the inputs — heavily regularized, low variance, but high bias. Ridge can be solved either by a closed-form equation (a small variant of the Normal equation) or by gradient descent, and Scikit-Learn exposes both: the Ridge class with a Cholesky-based solver for the closed form, or SGDRegressor with penalty='l2' for the gradient descent route. One detail matters for correctness: ridge, like most regularized models, is sensitive to feature scale, so the inputs need to be scaled (for example with StandardScaler) before fitting, or the penalty will not treat features fairly. Applied to a high-degree polynomial fit, increasing α visibly flattens the wiggly overfit curve into something far more reasonable — trading some bias for a large drop in variance.

blocks.title: Worked out: the matrix A, and why SGD gets alpha=0.1 / m
blocks.content:
In the closed-form Equation 4-9, A is the (n + 1) × (n + 1) identity matrix except with a 0 in the top-left cell, the cell that corresponds to the bias term, so the bias is not regularized.

The ridge cost in Equation 4-8 adds α/m times the sum of the squared feature weights. `SGDRegressor(penalty="l2")` adds alpha times the square of the ℓ2 norm of the weight vector, with no division by m. To make the two penalties equal, the code passes `alpha=0.1 / m`, which gives the same result as `Ridge(alpha=0.1)`. That is why the two predictions for an input of 1.5 nearly match: 1.55325833 from the Cholesky solver and 1.55302613 from SGD. For batch gradient descent, add 2αw / m to the part of the MSE gradient vector for the feature weights w, and add nothing to the gradient of the bias term.
