blocks.title: Key points
items: Neurons in convolutional layers connect only to small local regions called receptive fields rather than every pixel.
Zero padding surrounds inputs with zeros to maintain layer dimensions across convolutions.
Stride defines the step size between adjacent receptive fields and reduces layer spatial dimensions.
Filters represent reusable weight matrices that activate when detecting specific local visual patterns.
Applying a single weight filter across an input produces a two-dimensional feature map.

blocks.content:
A single two-dimensional filter can only detect one specific visual feature, such as a horizontal line or a sharp edge. To detect multiple visual characteristics simultaneously, a convolutional layer applies several distinct filters to its inputs, producing a three-dimensional output volume composed of stacked **feature maps**.

Each filter generates its own two-dimensional feature map, where every neuron represents the activation level of a specific feature at a given spatial location. Although individual feature maps operate in two dimensions, the overall layer output is three-dimensional because multiple feature maps are stacked together. Neurons within a single feature map share the exact same parameters, consisting of a kernel weight set and a **bias term**, which drastically reduces total parameter count and enables location-invariant feature detection. However, neurons across different feature maps utilize distinct sets of parameters.

As Figure 14-6 shows, a neuron's receptive field spans across all feature maps or channels of the preceding layer. For instance, consider an input RGB image with 3 color channels. If a convolutional layer applies a $3 \times 3$ kernel with a single filter, that filter contains $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$ weights plus 1 bias term. If the layer uses 32 independent filters instead, it produces 32 output feature maps, requiring $32 \times 28 = 896$ trainable parameters in total.

Equation 14-1 defines the mathematical output $z_{i,j,k}$ for a neuron at row $i$, column $j$, and feature map $k$. It computes a weighted sum over the receptive field height $f_h$, width $f_w$, and all $f_{n'}$ feature maps from the previous layer, then adds the filter bias $b_k$.

The crucial insight to remember is that while parameter sharing within each feature map keeps parameter counts low, a neuron's receptive field always extends across the entire depth dimension of the previous layer.

blocks.title: Same position, same inputs
blocks.content: In Equation 14-1, the input position depends only on the neuron's row and column: $i' = i \times s_h + u$ and $j' = j \times s_w + v$, where $s_h$ and $s_w$ are the vertical and horizontal strides. The feature map index $k$ does not appear in these formulas. As a result, all neurons located in the same row $i$ and column $j$ but in different feature maps of a layer are connected to the outputs of exactly the same neurons in the previous layer, across all of its feature maps. What differs between those neurons is their parameters: each feature map $k$ has its own weights $w_{u,v,k',k}$ and its own bias $b_k$, which you can think of as a knob that tweaks the overall brightness of feature map $k$.

blocks.title: Figure 14-6
blocks.caption: Two convolutional layers with multiple filters each (kernels), processing a color image
blocks.alt: Figure 14-6: Two convolutional layers with multiple filters each (kernels), processing a color image

blocks.title: Equation 14-1
blocks.caption: Computing the output of a neuron in a convolutional layer
blocks.latex: z_{i,j,k} = b_k + \sum_{u=0}^{f_h - 1} \sum_{v=0}^{f_w - 1} \sum_{k'=0}^{f_{n'} - 1} x_{i',j',k'} \times w_{u,v,k',k} \quad \text{with } \begin{cases} i' = i \times s_h + u \\ j' = j \times s_w + v \end{cases}

blocks.title: Key points
items: A convolutional layer uses multiple filters to produce a 3D output of stacked 2D feature maps.
Neurons within the same feature map share identical weights and bias parameters.
Neurons in different feature maps use different sets of parameters.
A neuron's receptive field extends across all feature maps or channels of the previous layer.
Equation 14-1 computes neuron outputs by summing weighted inputs across spatial dimensions and input channels.

blocks.content:
Standard fully connected layers struggle with spatial image structures and scale poorly with high-resolution inputs. To process visual data efficiently, spatial features must be extracted locally using trainable filters. Keras solves this problem using the `Conv2D` layer, which applies sliding convolutional kernels across 4D input tensors structured as `[batch_size, height, width, channels]`.

The layer operates by sliding local kernels of size `kernel_size` across the input image. The stride hyperparameter determines the step size of this movement, while padding options control border handling. Using default `padding="valid"` adds no extra zeros, causing feature maps to shrink based on kernel size. Using `padding="same"` pads the inputs with zeros so that output spatial dimensions match the input dimensions when `strides=1`. Figure 14-7 illustrates how `padding="valid"` reduces output spatial dimensions whereas `padding="same"` pads edges with zero values to preserve spatial dimensions.

Consider an input batch containing 2 cropped images of size $70 \times 120$ pixels with 3 RGB color channels, yielding a tensor shape of `[2, 70, 120, 3]`. Passing this tensor through a `Conv2D` layer configured with 32 filters, `kernel_size=7`, and `padding="valid"` produces an output tensor of shape `[2, 64, 114, 32]`. The spatial height shrinks by 6 pixels ($70 - 7 + 1 = 64$) and width shrinks by 6 pixels ($120 - 7 + 1 = 114$), while the final dimension expands to match the 32 feature maps.

The key insight to remember is that convolutional weights are shared across spatial dimensions, allowing `Conv2D` layers to process inputs of any height and width as long as the input color channels match the layer configuration.

blocks.title: The shapes of the kernels and biases
blocks.content: After the book creates `Conv2D(filters=32, kernel_size=7)` and applies it to the RGB images, `conv_layer.get_weights()` returns a kernels array of shape `(7, 7, 3, 32)` and a biases array of shape `(32,)`. The kernels array is 4D, with shape `[kernel_height, kernel_width, input_channels, output_channels]`: 7 × 7 is the filter size, 3 is the number of input color channels, and 32 is the number of output feature maps, which equals the number of filters. The biases array is 1D, with one bias per output channel. The height and width of the input images appear in neither shape, because all the neurons in an output feature map share the same weights. The kernels are initialized randomly and the biases start at zero.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf
from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_images

images = load_sample_images()["images"]
images = tf.keras.layers.CenterCrop(height=70, width=120)(images)
images = tf.keras.layers.Rescaling(scale=1 / 255)(images)

conv_layer = tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(filters=32, kernel_size=7, padding="same")
fmaps = conv_layer(images)

kernels, biases = conv_layer.get_weights()
print("Input shape:", images.shape)
print("Output shape:", fmaps.shape)
print("Kernels shape:", kernels.shape)
```

blocks.title: Key points
items: Input tensors to Keras Conv2D layers use a 4D shape formatted as batch size, height, width, and channels.
The default valid padding applies no zero-padding, shrinking spatial output dimensions based on filter size.
Setting padding to same adds zero-padding around borders to maintain input spatial dimensions when stride is 1.
Conv2D kernel weights depend only on filter size and channel counts, making them independent of input image dimensions.

items.term: Memory Requirements in Convolutional Neural Networks

blocks.content:
Training deep **convolutional neural networks** presents a significant hardware challenge because feature maps consume massive amounts of random-access memory. While convolutional layers generally contain far fewer parameters than fully connected layers, their intermediate activations require substantial storage. During the forward pass of model training, every layer produces intermediate outputs that must remain in memory until the backward pass completes, because the **backpropagation** algorithm relies on these preserved activations to compute parameter gradients.

During inference, memory can be freed immediately after computing the subsequent layer, requiring only enough RAM to hold two consecutive layers. However, during training, the network must retain the activations of all layers simultaneously. This cumulative memory footprint scales directly with both the size of the intermediate feature maps and the mini-batch size used during training.

Consider a concrete example featuring a single convolutional layer with 200 filters of size 5 by 5, operating with a stride of 1 and same padding on a 150 by 100 RGB image. The layer requires only 15,200 trainable parameters. However, its output consists of 200 feature maps of size 150 by 100. Using standard 32-bit floating-point numbers, one single image generates 12 megabytes of activation data. If training uses a mini-batch size of 100 images, this single layer consumes 1.2 gigabytes of RAM. Across a deep architecture with dozens of layers, total memory usage easily exceeds available GPU capacity.

The key insight to remember is that training memory is dominated by intermediate activations rather than model parameters, meaning that reducing batch size or using lower-precision float types is essential when facing **out-of-memory** errors.

blocks.title: Worked out: 15,200 parameters, 12 MB and 1.2 GB
blocks.content:
The layer has 200 filters of size 5 × 5, with stride 1 and "same" padding, applied to a 150 × 100 RGB image with 3 channels.

1. **Parameters:** each filter has 5 × 5 × 3 = 75 weights plus 1 bias term, so the layer holds (5 × 5 × 3 + 1) × 200 = 15,200 parameters.
2. **Computation:** each of the 200 feature maps contains 150 × 100 neurons, and each neuron computes a weighted sum of its 75 inputs, which is a total of 225 million float multiplications.
3. **Memory for one image:** with 32-bit floats, the output occupies 200 × 150 × 100 × 32 = 96 million bits, which is 12 MB.
4. **Memory for a batch:** if a training batch contains 100 instances, this one layer uses 100 × 12 MB = 1.2 GB of RAM.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Convolutional layers have relatively few parameters but generate large intermediate feature maps.
Training requires keeping all intermediate activations in RAM for backpropagation, whereas inference only requires holding two consecutive layers.
Activation memory footprint scales linearly with the mini-batch size.
Out-of-memory errors can be resolved by reducing mini-batch size, increasing stride, using 16-bit floats, or removing layers.

items.term: Pooling Layers in Convolutional Neural Networks

blocks.content:
Deep convolutional neural networks often struggle with extreme computational load, memory consumption, and overfitting when processing high-resolution feature maps. To solve this problem, **pooling layers** downsample input feature maps to shrink their spatial dimensions while preserving key features.

Unlike standard convolutional layers, neurons in a pooling layer do not learn any weights or bias parameters. Instead, a pooling neuron slides across a receptive field defined by a kernel size, stride, and padding setting, aggregating values using a deterministic function such as maximum or mean calculation. Each input channel is processed independently, meaning the depth of the volume remains unchanged.

As shown in **Figure 14-9**, consider a lower-left $2 \times 2$ receptive field with input values $1$, $5$, $3$, and $2$. Applying a **max pooling** layer with a $2 \times 2$ kernel and a stride of $2$ selects the maximum value, $5$, and drops the remaining three values. This downsampling step reduces both the height and width of the feature map by half, eliminating $75\%$ of the spatial inputs.

Beyond reducing parameters and computation, max pooling offers small-scale **translation invariance**. Because the maximum value in a window is retained regardless of slight shifts, minor spatial shifts in the input image frequently produce identical output maps. However, this loss of spatial resolution makes pooling unsuitable for dense prediction tasks like semantic segmentation, where exact spatial **equivariance** is required.

blocks.title: Invariance versus equivariance
blocks.content: Figure 14-10 sends three images A, B and C through a max pooling layer with a 2 × 2 kernel and stride 2; B and C are A shifted one and two pixels to the right. The outputs for A and B are identical, which is what **translation invariance** means. The output for C is shifted one pixel to the right, so there is still 50% invariance. Such invariance is useful in classification, where the prediction should not depend on these details. It is not always desirable, though. In **semantic segmentation**, the task of classifying each pixel according to the object it belongs to, an input translated one pixel to the right should give an output translated one pixel to the right. The goal there is **equivariance**: a small change to the inputs should lead to a corresponding small change in the output.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Pooling layers downsample feature maps to reduce computational cost, memory usage, and overfitting.
Pooling neurons possess no trainable weights and aggregate inputs using functions like max or mean.
Pooling operates on each feature map channel independently, preserving the total channel depth.
Max pooling provides small-scale translation invariance, which benefits image classification tasks.
The spatial reduction from pooling can harm tasks like semantic segmentation that demand exact location details.

blocks.content:
Convolutional neural networks require a mechanism to reduce spatial dimensions, lower computational costs, and gain invariance to small translations or transformations. **Pooling layers** address this challenge by downsampling feature maps through spatial aggregation operations.

In Keras, spatial pooling is typically performed using **max pooling** or **average pooling**. The standard `MaxPool2D` layer slides a kernel across spatial dimensions and extracts the maximum value within each window. By default, setting a pool size of 2 uses a stride of 2 and valid padding, halving both the height and width of the input maps. Max pooling is preferred over average pooling because it suppresses noise by preserving only the strongest feature signals, providing cleaner data to downstream layers.

Pooling can also operate along the depth (channel) axis rather than spatial axes. As shown in Figure 14-11, **depthwise max pooling** evaluates maximum values across groups of feature maps. This allows a network to achieve invariance against variations such as object rotation, thickness, or brightness, by selecting the most active filter response among a set of rotated patterns.

Finally, modern architectures often employ **global average pooling** near the network output. The `GlobalAvgPool2D` layer computes the mean across the entire height and width of each feature map. For a concrete example, if a batch of 2 RGB images with spatial dimensions of $28 \times 28$ (shape `[2, 28, 28, 3]`) is passed to a `GlobalAvgPool2D` layer, it reduces each spatial $28 \times 28$ matrix to its overall mean. The layer outputs a tensor of shape `(2, 3)`, representing the average intensity of the red, green, and blue channels for each image instance.

The key insight to remember is that while spatial max pooling compresses local dimensions, global average pooling condenses full feature maps into single summary values prior to final classification.

blocks.title: Global average pooling as a Lambda layer
blocks.content:
A global average pooling layer computes the mean of each entire feature map, like an average pooling layer whose kernel has the same spatial size as the inputs, so it outputs a single number per feature map and per instance. `tf.keras.layers.GlobalAvgPool2D()` is equivalent to a `Lambda` layer that computes the mean over the spatial dimensions, height (axis 1) and width (axis 2):

```python
global_avg_pool = tf.keras.layers.Lambda(
    lambda X: tf.reduce_mean(X, axis=[1, 2]))
```

Applied to the book's two 70 × 120 RGB sample images, the layer returns a tensor of shape `(2, 3)`: the mean intensity of red, green and blue for each image. The layer is extremely destructive, but it can be useful just before the output layer.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

# Spatial max pooling with a 2x2 kernel
max_pool = tf.keras.layers.MaxPool2D(pool_size=2)

# Global average pooling over spatial dimensions
global_avg_pool = tf.keras.layers.GlobalAvgPool2D()

# Custom depthwise max pooling layer
class DepthPool(tf.keras.layers.Layer):
    def __init__(self, pool_size=2, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.pool_size = pool_size
    def call(self, inputs):
        shape = tf.shape(inputs)
        groups = shape[-1] // self.pool_size
        new_shape = tf.concat([shape[:-1], [groups, self.pool_size]], axis=0)
        return tf.reduce_max(tf.reshape(inputs, new_shape), axis=-1)
```

blocks.title: Key points
items: MaxPool2D defaults to a stride equal to its pool size and uses valid padding.
Max pooling generally outperforms average pooling because it retains dominant features while filtering noise.
Depthwise max pooling enables invariance to transformations such as rotation by pooling across channel groups.
Global average pooling reduces each entire spatial feature map to a single mean value per channel.

blocks.content:
Standard dense networks struggle with image processing because raw pixel inputs contain massive numbers of parameters and discard spatial geometry. A **convolutional neural network (CNN)** solves this problem by structuring feature extraction hierarchically before applying fully connected classification layers.

As Figure 14-12 shows, a typical CNN architecture alternates between convolutional blocks and pooling layers before finishing with a regular feedforward network. Each convolutional layer applies filters followed by a **rectified linear unit (ReLU)** activation function to detect visual patterns. Next, a **pooling layer** reduces the spatial dimensions (height and width) of the representations. Stacking these operations shrinks spatial dimensions progressively while increasing channel depth. Stacking multiple small filters (such as two consecutive $3 \times 3$ kernels) is preferred over a single large filter (such as $5 \times 5$) because it uses fewer parameters and computations while enabling greater non-linearity. At the end of the feature extraction pipeline, a **Flatten layer** converts the multidimensional feature maps into a one-dimensional array, feeding regular dense layers capped by a **softmax** output layer.

Consider classifying a $28 \times 28$ grayscale image from Fashion MNIST. The network processes the input through a $7 \times 7$ convolution yielding 64 channels, then a max pooling layer with pool size 2 divides the spatial resolution to $14 \times 14$. Two subsequent $3 \times 3$ convolutions produce 128 channels, followed by another pooling step that halves the spatial dimensions to $7 \times 7$. Because pooling reduces the spatial footprint by a factor of 4 in area, the network safely doubles filter counts to 256 in the next stage without exploding computational cost. The flattened outputs pass through dense layers with 50% dropout to produce 10 class probabilities.

The core insight of standard CNN design is to trade spatial resolution for feature depth: as representations shrink in height and width, the network increases the number of feature channels to capture increasingly rich combinations of visual patterns.

blocks.title: When a large kernel is fine
blocks.content: A common mistake is to use convolution kernels that are too large. Instead of one convolutional layer with a 5 × 5 kernel, stack two layers with 3 × 3 kernels: the stack uses fewer parameters, requires fewer computations, and usually performs better. The one exception is the **first** convolutional layer. It can typically have a large kernel (e.g., 5 × 5), usually with a stride of 2 or more. This reduces the spatial dimension of the image without losing too much information, and since the input image generally has only three channels, the large kernel is not too costly. In the Fashion MNIST model, the first layer uses 64 fairly large 7 × 7 filters but keeps the default stride of 1, because the 28 × 28 input images are not very large.

blocks.caption: Typical CNN architecture

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
model = tf.keras.Sequential([
    DefaultConv2D(filters=64, kernel_size=7, input_shape=[28, 28, 1]),
    tf.keras.layers.MaxPool2D(),
    DefaultConv2D(filters=128),
    DefaultConv2D(filters=128),
    tf.keras.layers.MaxPool2D(),
    DefaultConv2D(filters=256),
    DefaultConv2D(filters=256),
    tf.keras.layers.MaxPool2D(),
    tf.keras.layers.Flatten(),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(units=128, activation="relu"),
    tf.keras.layers.Dropout(0.5),
    tf.keras.layers.Dense(units=10, activation="softmax")
])
```

blocks.title: Key points
items: Typical CNNs alternate between convolutional layers and pooling layers before finishing with dense layers.
Spatial dimensions decrease with depth while the number of feature channels increases.
Stacking two 3x3 convolutions requires fewer parameters and computations than using one 5x5 convolution.
Doubling feature maps after downsampling keeps compute and parameter footprints balanced.
Feature maps must be flattened into a 1D vector before entering fully connected dense layers.

items.term: Classic CNN Architectures: LeNet-5 and AlexNet

blocks.content:
Early image recognition models struggled to extract complex spatial patterns without overfitting on small datasets. To solve this problem, Yann LeCun introduced **LeNet-5** in 1998, establishing the classic convolutional network layout: alternating convolutional layers and pooling layers followed by fully connected dense layers. While LeNet-5 successfully recognized handwritten digits, deeper networks required more capacity and stronger regularization to prevent overfitting on large-scale datasets.

In 2012, the **AlexNet** architecture expanded upon LeNet-5 by introducing a significantly deeper structure. Unlike LeNet-5, AlexNet was the first network to stack multiple convolutional layers directly on top of one another before applying max pooling. It achieved superior generalization through two primary regularization techniques: applying a 50% dropout rate to its fully connected layers and utilizing **data augmentation**. As Figure 14-13 shows, data augmentation artificially expands a dataset by creating realistic variations of images through random shifting, horizontal flipping, and contrast modifications. This forces the model to remain invariant to changes in orientation, brightness, and position.

Additionally, AlexNet introduced a competitive normalization step called **local response normalization** (LRN). As Equation 14-2 shows, LRN calculates a normalized output $b_i$ by dividing a neuron's activation $a_i$ by a factor derived from the squared activations of neighboring feature maps within a depth radius $r$. For example, setting the hyperparameter $r = 5$ causes a strongly activated neuron to laterally inhibit neighboring neurons at the same spatial coordinates across adjacent feature maps. This biological inhibition encourages individual feature maps to specialize in distinct visual patterns.

The essential insight to remember is that scaling up network depth requires combining stacked convolutional layers with strong regularization methods, such as data augmentation and competitive normalization, to prevent severe overfitting.

blocks.title: Data augmentation done right, and the LRN radius
blocks.content:
**Data augmentation** artificially enlarges the training set by generating many realistic variants of each training instance, which reduces overfitting. Ideally, a human should not be able to tell whether an image was augmented. Simply adding white noise will not help, because the modifications should be learnable and white noise is not. As Figure 14-13 shows, you can slightly shift, rotate and resize every picture, which makes the model more tolerant to variations in the position, orientation and size of objects. Images with various contrasts make it tolerant to lighting, and horizontal flips work except for text and other asymmetrical objects.

In Equation 14-2, $r$ is the depth radius. For example, with $r = 2$ a strongly activated neuron inhibits the neurons located in the feature maps immediately above and below its own. AlexNet uses $r = 5$, $\alpha = 0.0001$, $\beta = 0.75$ and $k = 2$.

blocks.title: Figure 14-13
blocks.caption: Generating new training instances from existing ones
blocks.alt: Figure 14-13: Generating new training instances from existing ones

blocks.title: Equation 14-2
blocks.caption: Local response normalization (LRN)
blocks.latex: b_i = a_i \left( k + \alpha \sum_{j=j_{\text{low}}}^{j_{\text{high}}} {a_j}^2 \right)^{-\beta} \quad \text{with} \quad \begin{cases} j_{\text{high}} = \min \left( i + \frac{r}{2}, f_n - 1 \right) \\ j_{\text{low}} = \max \left( 0, i - \frac{r}{2} \right) \end{cases}

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow import keras

# Local Response Normalization implemented as a Keras layer
lrn_layer = keras.layers.Lambda(
    lambda x: tf.nn.local_response_normalization(
        x, depth_radius=5, bias=2.0, alpha=0.0001, beta=0.75
    )
)
```

blocks.title: Key points
items: LeNet-5 established the foundational CNN design using stacked convolution, average pooling, and dense layers.
AlexNet increased model capacity by stacking multiple convolutional layers directly on top of each other.
Data augmentation reduces overfitting by generating realistic variants of training images.
Local response normalization encourages feature map specialization through competitive lateral inhibition.

blocks.content:
Deep neural networks face heavy computational costs and overfitting risks when scaled up using traditional stacks of layers. To solve this efficiency problem, the **GoogLeNet** architecture introduces sub-networks called **inception modules**. These modules enable the network to capture multi-scale spatial patterns while keeping the parameter count low.

As Figure 14-14 demonstrates, an inception module feeds its input signal into four parallel branches simultaneously. The layers inside these paths utilize different kernel sizes, specifically $1 \times 1$, $3 \times 3$, and $5 \times 5$, alongside a max pooling layer. Because all four paths use a stride of 1 and standard same padding, every output feature map retains the exact height and width of the input. Consequently, a final depth concatenation layer stacks all output feature maps along the channel dimension.

A key innovation inside the inception module is the use of $1 \times 1$ convolutional layers. While a single pixel filter cannot extract spatial structures, it captures relationships across channel dimensions. Furthermore, when configured to output fewer feature maps than its input, a $1 \times 1$ convolution acts as a **bottleneck layer** that drastically reduces channel depth. For example, before running a costly $5 \times 5$ convolution on a high-dimensional feature map, a $1 \times 1$ convolution reduces the channel depth first, cutting down both parameter counts and memory footprint.

GoogLeNet combines nine of these inception modules into a single tall stack, as illustrated in Figure 14-15. Near the top of the network, a **global average pooling layer** computes the spatial mean of each feature map. This removes remaining spatial location details and eliminates the need for massive fully connected layers, reducing parameters to roughly 6 million—ten times fewer than AlexNet.

The single most important insight to remember is that $1 \times 1$ bottleneck convolutions allow deep networks to process multi-scale spatial features efficiently without parameter explosion.

blocks.title: VGGNet, the runner-up of 2014
blocks.content: The runner-up in the ILSVRC 2014 challenge, which GoogLeNet won, was **VGGNet**, developed by Karen Simonyan and Andrew Zisserman of the Visual Geometry Group (VGG) research lab at Oxford University. Unlike GoogLeNet with its inception modules, VGGNet has a very simple and classical architecture: 2 or 3 convolutional layers and a pooling layer, then again 2 or 3 convolutional layers and a pooling layer, and so on, for a total of 16 or 19 convolutional layers depending on the variant. It ends with a final dense network made of 2 hidden layers and the output layer. It uses small 3 × 3 filters, but it has many of them.

blocks.title: Key points
items: GoogLeNet uses inception modules to extract spatial patterns at multiple scales simultaneously.
The 1x1 convolutional layers act as bottleneck layers to reduce channel depth and lower parameter counts.
All parallel branches within an inception module use same padding and stride 1 so their outputs can be concatenated along the depth dimension.
Global average pooling replaces massive fully connected layers near the network output, drastically limiting overfitting.
GoogLeNet achieves high depth with roughly 6 million parameters, using ten times fewer parameters than AlexNet.

blocks.content:
Extremely deep neural networks traditionally suffer from training difficulties such as vanishing signals during backpropagation. As more layers are added, information and gradients fail to flow effectively through the entire network, causing performance to degrade instead of improving.

To solve this issue, **Residual Networks (ResNets)** introduce **skip connections** (or shortcut connections). As Figure 14-16 shows, a skip connection routes the input $x$ directly to the output of a group of layers, forcing the layers to learn a residual function $f(x) = h(x) - x$ rather than trying to fit the target function $h(x)$ from scratch. Because initial layer weights start near zero, the unit initially defaults to modeling an identity function ($h(x) \approx x$). As Figure 14-17 illustrates, this structure allows signals to pass uninterrupted across the entire stack, enabling gradients to backpropagate even if intermediate layers have not yet learned useful representations.

Consider a scenario where the network needs to change feature map dimensions inside a **residual unit**. When moving from 64 feature maps to 128 feature maps while halving the spatial dimensions using a stride of 2, the shape of input $x$ no longer matches the layer output $f(x)$. As shown in Figure 14-19, the architecture resolves this mismatch by passing the input through a $1 \times 1$ convolutional layer with a stride of 2 and 128 output maps before performing element-wise addition.

The essential insight of ResNets is that learning small residual adjustments to an identity mapping allows networks to scale up to hundreds of layers without gradient signals vanishing.

blocks.title: Bottleneck residual units in ResNet-152
blocks.content: ResNet-34 stacks 3 residual units (RUs) that output 64 feature maps, 4 RUs with 128 maps, 6 RUs with 256 maps and 3 RUs with 512 maps, and each RU holds two 3 × 3 convolutional layers. Deeper ResNets such as ResNet-152 use slightly different RUs. Instead of two 3 × 3 layers with, say, 256 feature maps, each RU has three convolutional layers: a 1 × 1 layer with just 64 feature maps (4 times fewer), which acts as a **bottleneck layer**, then a 3 × 3 layer with 64 feature maps, and finally a 1 × 1 layer with 256 feature maps (4 × 64) that restores the original depth. A bottleneck layer outputs fewer feature maps than its input, which cuts the computational cost and the number of parameters. ResNet-152 contains 3 such RUs with 256 maps, 8 with 512, 36 with 1,024 and 3 with 2,048.

Key points
items: Skip connections add the input directly to the output of a block of layers, enabling residual learning.
Initial weight values near zero make residual units model identity functions by default, accelerating early training.
Signals and gradients propagate cleanly through deep stacks even when intermediate layers fail to learn.
A 1x1 convolution with stride 2 matches spatial dimensions and channel counts when feature map sizes change.

blocks.content:
Standard convolutional layers attempt to process spatial patterns and cross-channel relationships simultaneously within the same set of 3D filters. This joint computation requires significant memory, processing power, and parameter count, which limits network efficiency when scaling up to very large datasets.

The **depthwise separable convolutional layer** solves this computational bottleneck by separating spatial feature extraction from cross-channel feature extraction. As Figure 14-20 illustrates, the operation is divided into two sequential stages. First, a depthwise stage applies a single, independent spatial filter to each individual input feature map to extract spatial patterns. Second, a pointwise stage uses a standard convolutional layer with $1 \times 1$ filters across all feature maps to combine the results and look exclusively for cross-channel patterns.

Consider an architecture like **Xception** (Extreme Inception), designed by François Chollet. Instead of using complex inception modules that only partially separate these operations, Xception fully replaces them with separable convolutions. The network begins with 2 standard convolutional layers to handle initial low-channel inputs, followed by 34 depthwise separable convolutional layers, max pooling layers, global average pooling, and a dense output layer. Because each depthwise step uses only one spatial filter per input channel, separable convolutions should not be placed directly after layers with very few channels, such as the initial 3-channel input image.

The core insight worth remembering is that separating spatial and cross-channel modeling reduces total parameters and computation cost while often achieving superior accuracy compared to standard convolutions.

blocks.title: Where inception modules sit, and the Keras layers
blocks.content:
Xception counts as a variant of GoogLeNet even though it contains no inception modules. An inception module contains convolutional layers with 1 × 1 filters, which look exclusively for cross-channel patterns, but the convolutional layers on top of them are regular layers that look for both spatial and cross-channel patterns. So an inception module is an intermediate between a regular convolutional layer, which considers the two kinds of pattern jointly, and a separable convolutional layer, which considers them separately. In practice, separable layers often perform better.

In Keras, `SeparableConv2D` is a drop-in replacement for `Conv2D`. Keras also offers `DepthwiseConv2D`, which implements only the first part of a depthwise separable layer: applying one spatial filter per input feature map.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow import keras

# Drop-in replacement for Conv2D
model = keras.models.Sequential([
    # Start with standard convolution for few channels
    keras.layers.Conv2D(32, kernel_size=3, input_shape=[228, 228, 3]),
    keras.layers.Conv2D(64, kernel_size=3),
    # Use separable convolutions for remaining main network
    keras.layers.SeparableConv2D(128, kernel_size=3, activation="relu"),
    keras.layers.SeparableConv2D(128, kernel_size=3, activation="relu"),
    keras.layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D(),
    keras.layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")
])
```

blocks.title: Key points
items: Standard convolutions search for spatial and cross-channel patterns at the same time.
Depthwise separable convolutions split processing into spatial filtering per channel and $1 \times 1$ pointwise convolutions.
Separable convolutions use fewer parameters and memory while frequently outperforming standard convolutions.
The Xception network relies heavily on 34 separable convolutional layers after starting with 2 standard convolutions.
Separable convolutions should be avoided immediately after layers with very few channels.

blocks.content:
Standard convolutional neural networks treat all output feature maps equally, missing inter-channel relationships and contextual dependencies across features. To solve this limitation, the **Squeeze-and-Excitation Network (SENet)** introduces small neural network modules called **SE blocks** that recalibrate feature maps by dynamically weighting channels based on their global context.

As Figure 14-23 shows, an SE block processes feature maps through three sequential operations. First, a **global average pooling** layer compresses spatial dimensions by calculating the mean activation for each feature map, squeezing spatial details into a single depth vector. Next, a dense hidden layer with **ReLU** activation reduces the vector size (typically by a factor of 16), creating a low-dimensional bottleneck embedding that forces the model to learn inter-channel relationships. Finally, a dense output layer with **sigmoid** activation expands the vector back to the original channel count, producing a set of weights strictly between 0 and 1. As shown in Figure 14-22, the original feature maps are multiplied element-wise by this recalibration vector to scale down irrelevant features while preserving informative ones.

Consider an SE block receiving 256 feature maps. Global average pooling outputs 256 summary values. The bottleneck layer compresses these 256 numbers down to 16 neurons. The final output layer expands the 16 numbers back to 256 weights (such as 0.0, 1.0, and 0.3). Multiplying the 256 original feature maps by these weights suppresses background noise while highlighting target channels. Figure 14-21 demonstrates how SE blocks attach seamlessly to standard architectures like Inception modules or ResNet units.

The central insight to remember is that SE blocks dynamically recalibrate feature channels by modeling inter-channel dependencies, ignoring spatial patterns to focus entirely on depth relationships.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow import keras

def se_block(inputs, reduction_ratio=16):
    channels = inputs.shape[-1]
    # Squeeze step: global average pooling
    squeeze = keras.layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(inputs)
    # Excitation step: bottleneck dense layers
    bottleneck = keras.layers.Dense(channels // reduction_ratio, activation="relu")(squeeze)
    excitation = keras.layers.Dense(channels, activation="sigmoid")(bottleneck)
    # Recalibrate original inputs via element-wise multiplication
    recalibrated = keras.layers.Reshape((1, 1, channels))(excitation)
    return keras.layers.Multiply()([inputs, recalibrated])
```

blocks.title: Key points
items: SENet enhances neural networks by adding SE blocks to recalibrate channel feature maps dynamically.
An SE block ignores spatial patterns to focus exclusively on inter-channel depth relationships.
The squeeze step uses global average pooling to condense spatial dimensions into channel summary values.
The excitation step compresses values into a low-dimensional embedding before expanding them with sigmoid activation.
Original feature maps are multiplied by the output recalibration vector to suppress irrelevant features.

blocks.content:
Designing high-performing convolutional neural networks often requires scaling existing architectures to match larger compute budgets. Traditionally, practitioners increased network depth by adding layers, network width by adding filters, or image resolution independently. However, scaling only one dimension yields diminishing returns and inefficient resource utilization because a larger image requires both deeper networks to capture receptive fields and wider networks to extract granular features.

To solve this issue, **EfficientNet** introduced **compound scaling**, a principled method that jointly scales depth, width, and resolution using a fixed set of scaling coefficients. The total compute budget is represented by a parameter $\phi$, where increasing $\phi$ by 1 doubles the available floating-point operations ($2^\phi$). The network depth, width, and resolution are scaled by factors of $\alpha^\phi$, $\beta^\phi$, and $\gamma^\phi$, respectively. The constants $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ are constrained such that $\alpha \cdot \beta^2 \cdot \gamma^2 \approx 2$, ensuring that total compute scales predictably with $2^\phi$.

For a concrete example, the authors established the baseline model **EfficientNetB0** and ran a grid search with $\phi = 1$ to discover the optimal factors: $\alpha = 1.2$ for depth, $\beta = 1.1$ for width, and $\gamma = 1.1$ for resolution. When moving to larger compute budgets by increasing $\phi$, these precise exponents scale the baseline model up through variants named **EfficientNetB1** to **EfficientNetB7**. By maintaining this optimal balance across dimensions, EfficientNet models achieve superior accuracy across compute budgets compared to models scaled along a single dimension.

The key insight behind compound scaling is that network depth, width, and input resolution must be scaled together in balanced proportions to maximize accuracy for a given compute budget.

blocks.title: ResNeXt, DenseNet and CSPNet
blocks.content:
The book presents EfficientNet in a list of other noteworthy CNN architectures:

- **ResNeXt** improves the residual units of ResNet. Each unit is made of many parallel stacks (e.g., 32 stacks) of 3 convolutional layers, but the first two layers in each stack use only a few filters (e.g., just four), so the overall number of parameters stays the same as in ResNet. The outputs of all the stacks are added together and passed to the next unit, along with the skip connection.
- **DenseNet** is built from dense blocks of densely connected convolutional layers: the output of each layer is fed as input to every later layer in the same block. For example, layer 4 takes the depthwise concatenation of the outputs of layers 1, 2 and 3.
- **CSPNet** is similar to DenseNet, but part of each dense block's input is concatenated directly to that block's output, without going through the block.

blocks.title: Key points
items: EfficientNet uses compound scaling to jointly increase network depth, width, and input image resolution.
The compute budget parameter increases logarithmically such that doubling compute increases the budget exponent by one.
Scaling coefficients derived from grid search ensure proportional allocation of resources across all three network dimensions.
Balanced compound scaling enables EfficientNet to achieve high accuracy while using fewer parameters and floating-point operations.

blocks.content:
Selecting a **convolutional neural network** (CNN) architecture requires balancing multiple constraints rather than simply picking the model with the highest performance score. Real-world applications often operate under strict limits, such as memory capacity on mobile devices, low execution time requirements, or hardware limitations like running on a central processing unit (CPU) versus a graphics processing unit (GPU). Consequently, developers must evaluate trade-offs between validation accuracy, total parameter count, disk storage footprint, and execution speed.

Pretrained models offered in deep learning frameworks provide a clear view of these performance trade-offs. While larger models generally yield higher accuracy, they also require significantly more storage memory and computational power. However, newer network designs frequently achieve better efficiency by outperforming older, larger architectures in both storage size and classification precision. Despite this efficiency, older models may still be preferred in specific deployment scenarios if their specialized structure allows them to execute faster on particular hardware target devices.

Consider a scenario where an engineer must choose between **EfficientNetB2** and **InceptionV3** for an edge deployment. EfficientNetB2 requires only 36 megabytes of storage space and achieves an 80.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with 9.2 million parameters. In contrast, InceptionV3 occupies 92 megabytes of storage and achieves a lower top-1 accuracy of 77.9% with 23.9 million parameters. While EfficientNetB2 appears superior in both accuracy and size, InceptionV3 runs nearly twice as fast on a standard CPU. If the deployment target relies strictly on CPU inference and demands minimal latency, InceptionV3 becomes the more suitable option.

The core insight to remember is that model selection is driven by operational trade-offs, where efficiency and target hardware speed are just as vital as top accuracy.

blocks.title: More figures from Table 14-3
blocks.content:
Table 14-3 lists pretrained Keras models by size, with their top-1 and top-5 ImageNet validation accuracy and their parameter count. Six of its rows:

- MobileNetV2: 14 MB, 71.3% top-1, 90.1% top-5, 3.5M parameters (the smallest in the table)
- EfficientNetB2: 36 MB, 80.1% top-1, 94.9% top-5, 9.2M parameters
- InceptionV3: 92 MB, 77.9% top-1, 93.7% top-5, 23.9M parameters
- ResNet50V2: 98 MB, 76.0% top-1, 93.0% top-5, 25.6M parameters
- ResNet101V2: 171 MB, 77.2% top-1, 93.8% top-5, 44.7M parameters
- EfficientNetB7: 256 MB, 84.3% top-1, 97.0% top-5, 66.7M parameters (the most accurate)

Speed tells a different story. InceptionV3 is almost twice as fast as EfficientNetB2 on a CPU, InceptionResNetV2 is fast on a CPU, and ResNet50V2 and ResNet101V2 are blazingly fast on a GPU.

```python
import tensorflow as tf

# Load a lightweight model for constrained environments
mobile_model = tf.keras.applications.MobileNetV2(
    weights="imagenet", include_top=True

# Load an efficient high-accuracy model for higher compute budgets
```

blocks.title: Key points
items: Choosing a CNN architecture requires balancing accuracy against model size, memory, and hardware latency.
Larger neural network models generally provide higher accuracy, but newer architectures can achieve better results with fewer parameters.
Model speed varies significantly depending on whether inference runs on a CPU or a GPU.
Older network architectures may remain useful if they offer faster execution times on specific hardware configurations.

blocks.content:
Deep neural networks often suffer from vanishing gradients, making them extremely difficult to train as depth increases. **Residual Networks** (ResNet) solve this problem by introducing **skip connections**, which allow input signals to bypass intermediate transformation layers and flow directly through the network. Building a complex architecture like ResNet-34 from scratch requires a modular approach so that repeated structures can be reused cleanly.

To construct ResNet-34 in Keras, we first define a custom layer class called **ResidualUnit**. This class encapsulates the main path, which consists of two convolutional layers paired with **Batch Normalization** and a ReLU activation function. If the unit reduces spatial dimensions using a stride greater than one, the skip connection path uses a 1x1 convolution to adjust the shape and channel count of the input so it can be added to the output of the main path.

Consider an input tensor with shape 224x224 and 3 color channels. The architecture begins with an initial 7x7 convolutional layer using 64 filters and a stride of 2, followed by max pooling, which reduces the spatial dimensions to 56x56. Next, a loop stacks 16 residual units: 3 with 64 filters, 4 with 128, 6 with 256 and 3 with 512 (the 34 in ResNet-34 counts the network's convolutional layers and its fully connected layer, not the residual units). Whenever the filter count doubles, the stride is set to 2 to downsample the spatial dimensions. Finally, a **Global Average Pooling** layer reduces each feature map to a single scalar before feeding into a dense layer with a **softmax** activation function for final class predictions.

The key insight worth remembering is that custom layers in Keras allow complex functional subgraphs like residual blocks to be abstracted into reusable objects, enabling deep architectures to be constructed using simple high-level APIs.

blocks.title: Worked out: from 224 × 224 down to 56 × 56
blocks.content:
The model starts with `DefaultConv2D(64, kernel_size=7, strides=2, input_shape=[224, 224, 3])`, and `DefaultConv2D` uses "same" padding. Batch normalization and ReLU follow, which do not change the size, and then comes `MaxPool2D(pool_size=3, strides=2, padding="same")`. With "same" padding, the output size is the input size divided by the stride, rounded up.

1. The 7 × 7 convolution with stride 2 gives 224 ÷ 2 = 112, so the feature maps are 112 × 112 with 64 channels.
2. The 3 × 3 max pooling with stride 2 gives 112 ÷ 2 = 56, so the first residual unit receives 56 × 56 feature maps.

The loop over `[64] * 3 + [128] * 4 + [256] * 6 + [512] * 3` then adds 16 residual units. The first unit at 128, 256 and 512 filters uses stride 2, which halves the maps again to 28 × 28, 14 × 14 and 7 × 7.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
class ResidualUnit(tf.keras.layers.Layer):
    def __init__(self, filters, strides=1, activation="relu", **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.activation = tf.keras.activations.get(activation)
        self.main_layers = [
            DefaultConv2D(filters, strides=strides),
            tf.keras.layers.BatchNormalization(),
            self.activation,
            DefaultConv2D(filters),
            tf.keras.layers.BatchNormalization()
        ]
        self.skip_layers = []
        if strides > 1:
            self.skip_layers = [
                DefaultConv2D(filters, kernel_size=1, strides=strides),
                tf.keras.layers.BatchNormalization()
            ]
```

blocks.title: Key points
items: Custom Keras layers simplify the creation of repeating architectural blocks such as residual units.
Skip connections add the original input to the output of main convolutional layers to preserve gradient flow.
When spatial dimensions change due to stride, the skip path uses a 1x1 convolution to match shapes.
ResNet-34 stacks residual units across groups of 64, 128, 256, and 512 filters using a simple loop.

blocks.content:
Training a large convolutional neural network from scratch requires immense computational resources and massive datasets. Building complex architectures such as ResNet-50 manually is both time-consuming and prone to errors. Pretrained models solve this issue by offering existing architectures alongside weights already trained on large-scale datasets.

To use a pretrained network from the `tf.keras.applications` package, you load the model with your chosen weights. For example, loading **ResNet-50** with ImageNet weights provides a model ready to classify images into 1,000 standard object categories. Before feeding input data into the model, the images must match the required dimensions and pixel scaling expected by that specific architecture. ResNet-50 expects input images to have a resolution of 224 by 224 pixels. You can achieve this by passing raw images through a resizing layer.

After resizing, you must preprocess the pixel values using the model's dedicated preprocessing function. For instance, `tf.keras.applications.resnet50.preprocess_input` converts pixel values ranging from 0 to 255 into the specific numerical distribution expected by ResNet-50. Once preprocessed, passing two sample images into `model.predict()` yields a output matrix with two rows and 1,000 columns, where each column represents a class probability score. Calling `decode_predictions()` translates these numerical predictions into human-readable class names and confidence percentages. Passing sample images through this pipeline might classify the first image as a palace with 54.69% probability and the second as a vase with 32.66% probability.

The essential insight is that **pretrained models** allow instant access to state-of-the-art vision classifiers, requiring only specific image resizing and model-matched preprocessing steps.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras.datasets.fashion_mnist import load_data
from tensorflow.keras.applications.resnet50 import ResNet50, preprocess_input, decode_predictions

model = ResNet50(weights="imagenet")

images = tf.keras.utils.load_img("sample.jpg") # load sample
images_array = tf.keras.utils.img_to_array(images)
images_resized = tf.keras.layers.Resizing(height=224, width=224, crop_to_aspect_ratio=True)([images_array])
inputs = preprocess_input(images_resized)

Y_proba = model.predict(inputs)
top_K = decode_predictions(Y_proba, top=3)
```

blocks.title: Key points
items: Pretrained vision networks with optimized weights are available directly within the `tf.keras.applications` module.
Input images must be resized to match the exact dimensions expected by the specific network architecture, such as 224 by 224 pixels for ResNet-50.
Each network architecture provides a dedicated `preprocess_input()` function to scale pixel values into its expected numerical format.
The `decode_predictions()` helper function converts output prediction probabilities into human-readable class names and confidence scores.

blocks.content:
Training deep convolutional neural networks from scratch requires massive datasets and compute resources. When working with small datasets containing only a few thousand images, training a network from scratch often leads to severe overfitting. **Transfer learning** solves this problem by reusing the learned lower-level feature extractors of a model trained on a massive dataset, such as ImageNet, and adapting them to a new task.

To implement transfer learning, we load a pretrained base model like Xception without its final classification head by setting `include_top=False`. We then append custom task-specific layers, typically a **global average pooling** layer followed by a dense output layer matching our target class count. Before initial training, we freeze the weights of the base model by setting the `trainable` attribute of its layers to `False`. Freezing prevents the large, randomly initialized gradients of our custom top layers from destroying the pretrained representations. After training the new top layers until their accuracy stabilizes, we can unfreeze some of the upper layers of the base model and fine-tune them together with the top layers using a reduced learning rate.

For example, when classifying a small flowers dataset of 3,670 images into 5 categories, an Xception base with frozen weights is fitted for 3 epochs at a learning rate of 0.1, reaching about 80% validation accuracy. Unfreezing layers 56 and above and continuing training for 10 epochs with a smaller learning rate of 0.01 increases the model accuracy to roughly 92%.

The key insight is that freezing pretrained layers protects useful visual features during initial training, while subsequent fine-tuning with a lower learning rate safely adapts high-level feature representations to the target task.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

base_model = tf.keras.applications.xception.Xception(
    weights="imagenet", include_top=False
)
avg = tf.keras.layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(base_model.output)
output = tf.keras.layers.Dense(5, activation="softmax")(avg)
model = tf.keras.Model(inputs=base_model.input, outputs=output)

for layer in base_model.layers:
    layer.trainable = False

optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=0.1, momentum=0.9)
model.compile(loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", optimizer=optimizer)
```

blocks.title: Key points
items: Transfer learning reuses feature extraction layers from a pretrained model to prevent overfitting on small datasets.
Setting include_top=False removes the original classification layers so custom task layers can be attached.
Pretrained layers must initially be frozen to prevent randomly initialized top weights from ruining existing features.
Fine-tuning unfrozen base layers requires recompiling the model and using a much lower learning rate.

blocks.content:
Standard image classification models identify what object is present in an image, but they do not identify where that object is located. To solve this problem, we perform **classification and localization**, which predicts both the object class and a bounding box around the main object.

To implement this, we frame localization as a regression task. A bounding box requires four numeric outputs: the center horizontal coordinate, the center vertical coordinate, the width, and the height. In a neural network architecture, a feature extraction base (such as a pre-trained Xception model) feeds into a global average pooling layer. We then add two separate output layers attached to this pooling layer: a classification layer with a softmax activation function to output class probabilities, and a localization layer with four linear units to output the bounding box parameters. All four bounding box parameters are normalized to fall between 0 and 1 relative to the image dimensions.

During training, the model uses a combined loss function. For instance, we can assign a loss weight of 0.8 to sparse categorical cross-entropy for classification and 0.2 to mean squared error (MSE) for localization. Suppose the predicted bounding box has coordinates $(0.5, 0.5, 0.4, 0.4)$ and the true label box has coordinates $(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5)$. The network computes the MSE loss on these four values to update the regression head.

While MSE works well for optimization during training, it is not an intuitive metric for assessing spatial overlap. Instead, model performance for bounding box accuracy is evaluated using **Intersection over Union (IoU)**, as shown in Figure 14-24. The **IoU** metric measures the area of overlap between the predicted box and the ground-truth box divided by the total area covered by both boxes combined.

blocks.title: Preparing the data, and the square-root trick
blocks.content: To train the model, you need a dataset whose items are batches of preprocessed images along with their class labels and their bounding boxes. Each item should be a tuple of the form `(images, (class_labels, bounding_boxes))`: the images are the input, and the inner pair matches the model's two outputs. The bounding boxes should be normalized so that the horizontal and vertical coordinates, as well as the height and width, all range from 0 to 1. It is also common to predict the square root of the height and width rather than the height and width directly. That way, a 10-pixel error for a large bounding box is not penalized as much as a 10-pixel error for a small bounding box.

blocks.caption: IoU metric for bounding boxes

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
base_model = tf.keras.applications.xception.Xception(
    weights="imagenet", include_top=False
)
avg = tf.keras.layers.GlobalAveragePooling2D()(base_model.output)
class_output = tf.keras.layers.Dense(n_classes, activation="softmax")(avg)
loc_output = tf.keras.layers.Dense(4)(avg)
model = tf.keras.Model(
    inputs=base_model.input, outputs=[class_output, loc_output]
)
model.compile(
    loss=["sparse_categorical_crossentropy", "mse"],
    loss_weights=[0.8, 0.2],
    optimizer=optimizer,
    metrics=["accuracy"],
)
```

blocks.title: Key points
items: Object localization is framed as a regression task that predicts four continuous values for a bounding box.
A dual-output network architecture predicts object classes and bounding box coordinates simultaneously.
Bounding box coordinates and dimensions are normalized between 0 and 1 for consistent regression targets.
Mean Squared Error (MSE) is commonly used to train the regression output, while Intersection over Union (IoU) evaluates bounding box overlap accuracy.

blocks.content:
Standard image classification models assume a single target object is centered within an image. When an image contains multiple objects at arbitrary positions, standard classification networks fail to localize and identify every instance. To solve this problem, early computer vision systems used the **sliding-CNN** approach to locate and categorize multiple targets systematically.

This technique divides an image into a regular grid and slides a bounding window across all possible regions. At each step, a trained Convolutional Neural Network evaluates the cropped sub-image to predict class probabilities, bounding box coordinates, and an **objectness score**. The objectness score represents the estimated probability that an object is centered inside that local window, typically predicted using a single dense unit with a sigmoid activation function. As shown in Figure 14-25, a window slides across $3 \times 3$ regions of a $5 \times 7$ grid, outputting predictions at each location. A window centered over a rose produces a high objectness score and bounding box, whereas a window over background pixels yields a low objectness score, allowing the model to ignore invalid predictions.

Because overlapping sliding windows frequently detect the same object multiple times, postprocessing is necessary. Systems apply **non-max suppression** by first discarding boxes below a minimum objectness threshold. Next, the algorithm selects the box with the highest objectness score and removes all remaining overlapping boxes that exceed a chosen Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold, such as 60%. This loop repeats until only distinct bounding boxes remain.

The essential insight is that evaluating candidate regions across spatial grids enables multi-object detection, but redundant predictions must be filtered out using non-max suppression.

blocks.title: Worked out: 15 predictions, and the cost
blocks.content:
In Figure 14-25 the image is chopped into a 5 × 7 grid, and the CNN looks at every 3 × 3 region.

1. Vertically, a window 3 cells tall fits in 5 − 3 + 1 = 3 positions.
2. Horizontally, a window 3 cells wide fits in 7 − 3 + 1 = 5 positions.
3. That gives a 3 × 5 grid of 15 predicted bounding boxes, each with its class probabilities and objectness score.

A predicted box may exceed the boundary of its 3 × 3 region: even when the CNN cannot see the bottom part of a rose, it can make a reasonable guess about where that part is. Since objects vary in size, you may slide the CNN again across larger 4 × 4 regions. The approach works pretty well, but it requires running the CNN many times (15 times in this example), so it is quite slow.

blocks.alt: Figure 14-25: Detecting multiple objects by sliding a CNN across the image

blocks.title: Key points
items: Object detection requires both localizing and classifying multiple objects within an image.
The sliding-CNN approach shifts a classification window across spatial grid regions to generate candidate bounding boxes.
An objectness score estimates whether an object is centered in the current window and allows filtering out empty regions.
Non-max suppression removes redundant, highly overlapping bounding boxes based on objectness scores and IoU thresholds.

blocks.content:
Standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs) rely on dense layers at their output. These dense layers impose a strict constraint: the network can only accept input images of a fixed spatial resolution because each dense neuron requires a fixed number of weights matching the exact spatial size of the input features. This fixed-size restriction prevents traditional CNNs from processing images of arbitrary sizes in a single pass.

To solve this limitation, **fully convolutional networks** (FCNs) replace the traditional dense output layers with equivalent convolutional layers. A dense layer with $N$ neurons sitting above a spatial feature map of size $H \times W$ can be directly converted into a convolutional layer. This converted layer uses $N$ filters, each of size $H \times W$, with valid padding. Because a spatial convolution computes the exact same weighted sums over local regions, the mathematical output of this convolutional layer is identical to the output of the dense layer. However, unlike dense layers, convolutional filters can slide over spatial inputs of any size.

As Figure 14-26 shows, feeding a larger image into an FCN scales up the spatial size of the feature maps throughout the network. For example, consider a network trained on $224 \times 224$ images whose bottleneck feature map is $7 \times 7$. Replacing its 10-unit dense layer with a convolutional layer using 10 filters of size $7 \times 7$ yields a single $1 \times 1$ spatial grid containing 10 predictions. If we instead feed this FCN a larger $448 \times 448$ image, the bottleneck feature map expands to $14 \times 14$. The final convolutional layer with valid padding then computes predictions across an $8 \times 8$ spatial grid ($14 - 7 + 1 = 8$). Each of these 64 grid positions contains the 10 prediction values for that spatial region.

The key insight to remember is that replacing dense layers with equivalent convolutional layers allows a neural network to process images of any spatial resolution in a single forward pass, efficiently sliding predictions across larger inputs.

blocks.caption: The same fully convolutional network processing a small image (left) and a large one
blocks.alt: Figure 14-26: The same fully convolutional network processing a small image (left) and a large one

blocks.title: Key points
items: Dense layers require fixed spatial input shapes because their weight matrices have a static size.
A dense layer converts to a convolutional layer by setting filter count to unit count and filter size to the feature map size with valid padding.
Fully convolutional networks consist entirely of convolutional and pooling layers, accepting arbitrary image dimensions.
Processing larger images in an FCN outputs spatial grids of predictions instead of single vector outputs.

items.term: The You Only Look Once Object Detection Model

blocks.content:
Standard object detection systems often rely on multi-step pipelines that propose candidate regions before running full classification networks. This two-stage approach causes significant processing delays and prevents real-time video analysis. The **You Only Look Once** (YOLO) architecture solves this efficiency problem by treating object detection as a single regression task, predicting bounding boxes and class probabilities directly from an image in one forward pass.

To accomplish this, YOLO divides an image into a grid of cells. Each grid cell is responsible for detecting any object whose bounding box center falls within that specific cell. The coordinates of the bounding box are defined relative to the cell, ranging from (0, 0) at the top-left to (1, 1) at the bottom-right, although the overall width and height of the bounding box can extend across surrounding grid cells. To handle multiple objects with nearby centers, each grid cell predicts two distinct bounding boxes alongside their corresponding confidence scores, known as **objectness scores**.

For example, imagine a single grid cell containing the center points for both a tall person and a wide car. The grid cell generates two bounding boxes: a narrow vertical box for the person and a wide horizontal box for the car. The model outputs a single class probability distribution per grid cell, such as predicting high probabilities for both person and car classes. During postprocessing, the system evaluates how well the geometry of each predicted bounding box matches the spatial regions of the class probability map, correctly matching the vertical box to the person class and the horizontal box to the car class.

The key insight behind YOLO is that framing detection as a single spatial grid evaluation yields exceptional processing speed, enabling real-time detection on video streams without sacrificing overall accuracy.

blocks.title: Look-once models versus Faster R-CNN
blocks.content: YOLO is so fast that it can run in real time on a video. Like a fully convolutional network, it processes the whole image only once instead of running a CNN on many separate regions, and SSD and EfficientDet are also "look once" detection models. **Faster R-CNN** is more complex. The image first goes through a CNN, then the output is passed to a region proposal network (RPN) that proposes the bounding boxes most likely to contain an object, and finally a classifier is run for each proposed bounding box, based on the cropped output of the CNN. A look-once model skips those separate proposal and per-box classification stages and makes all of its predictions in a single pass.

blocks.title: Key points
items: YOLO processes an entire image in a single pass by dividing it into a spatial grid.
A grid cell predicts objects only if the center of their bounding box falls inside that cell.
Each grid cell outputs two bounding boxes with objectness scores and one class probability distribution.
Bounding box coordinates are normalized relative to the cell, but box dimensions can extend beyond cell boundaries.
Postprocessing matches individual bounding boxes to class probability map regions to resolve final object labels.

blocks.content:
Object tracking in video streams is challenging because objects move, change orientation, alter appearance under different lighting, and become temporarily occluded. Simple detection models treat each frame independently, which makes maintaining consistent identity labels across consecutive frames difficult. The **DeepSORT** algorithm solves this association problem by combining classical state estimation algorithms with modern deep learning representations.

DeepSORT operates using three main components working together. First, it uses a **Kalman filter** to predict the expected position of an existing target in the current frame, relying on the assumption that objects generally maintain constant velocities. Next, a **deep learning model** generates appearance feature embeddings for newly detected objects, allowing the system to measure visual similarity between existing targets and new bounding boxes. Finally, the **Hungarian algorithm** computes an optimal assignment that maps new detections to tracked objects by simultaneously minimizing positional distance and visual discrepancy.

To understand this interaction, consider a scenario where a red ball and a blue ball collide and bounce off each other in opposite directions. Based strictly on prior motion vectors, the Kalman filter predicts that both balls will continue straight, effectively passing through each other. If the system evaluated only bounding box positions, the matching algorithm would incorrectly swap their identities after the bounce. However, because DeepSORT incorporates the appearance resemblance score from its deep learning model, the matching step recognizes that the red object's visual appearance matches its original track rather than the blue one, correctly preserving their identities despite the abrupt trajectory change.

The essential insight of DeepSORT is that combining motion estimation with visual feature embeddings prevents tracking errors during sudden directional changes or occlusions.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Object tracking maintains consistent identities across video frames despite motion, scale changes, and occlusions.
Kalman filters estimate future positions by assuming objects move at a constant velocity.
Deep learning models extract visual embeddings to evaluate resemblance between detections and tracked objects.

blocks.content:
Standard convolutional neural networks downsample images through strided convolutions and pooling layers. While this helps identify global object presence, it destroys spatial resolution, making precise pixel-level localization impossible. **Semantic segmentation** solves this problem by classifying every individual pixel into an object category, such as road, car, or sky.

To restore lost spatial resolution, Fully Convolutional Networks (FCNs) use **transposed convolutional layers** for upsampling. As Figure 14-28 shows, a transposed convolution stretches an input tensor by inserting zeros between elements before applying a standard convolution with learnable parameters. However, directly upsampling a heavily downsampled feature map (e.g., by a factor of 32) yields blurry predictions.

To recover fine spatial details, architectures introduce **skip connections** from earlier, higher-resolution layers. As shown in Figure 14-29, an FCN upsamples its bottleneck feature map by a factor of 2, adds the higher-resolution feature map from a lower layer, and then upsamples the combined result by a factor of 16 to recover the full input resolution.

The essential insight is that combining deep semantic features from higher layers with fine spatial details from lower layers via skip connections enables accurate pixel-level classification.

blocks.title: Instance segmentation, strides and dilation
blocks.content:
In semantic segmentation, different objects of the same class are not distinguished: all the bicycles in Figure 14-27 end up as one big lump of pixels. **Instance segmentation** is similar, but each object is distinguished from the others, so it identifies each individual bicycle. Mask R-CNN does this by extending Faster R-CNN with a pixel mask for each bounding box.

In a transposed convolutional layer (`Conv2DTranspose`), the stride defines how much the input is stretched, not the size of the filter steps, so the larger the stride, the larger the output. Setting `dilation_rate` to 2 or more on a convolutional layer inserts rows and columns of zeros into the filter: a 1 × 3 filter `[[1,2,3]]` with a dilation rate of 4 becomes `[[1, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 3]]`. The layer gets a larger receptive field at no computational price and with no extra parameters.

blocks.title: python example
blocks.content:
```python
import tensorflow as tf

# Transposed convolution to upsample spatial resolution by a factor of 2
upsample_layer = tf.keras.layers.Conv2DTranspose(
    filters=64,
    kernel_size=3,
    strides=2,
    padding="same",
    activation="relu"
)

# À-trous (dilated) convolution for expanded receptive field
dilated_layer = tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(
    filters=64,
    kernel_size=3,
    dilation_rate=2,
    padding="same",
    activation="relu"
)
```

blocks.title: Key points
items: Semantic segmentation classifies every pixel into a class without separating individual object instances.
Strided layers in traditional CNNs cause loss of fine spatial resolution.
Transposed convolutional layers perform trainable upsampling by stretching inputs with zeros.
Skip connections combine high-level semantic features with high-resolution lower-layer outputs.
Dilated convolutions increase the receptive field without adding extra parameters or downsampling.

sections.title: Chapter 15: Processing Sequences Using RNNs and CNNs

blocks.content:
Standard feedforward neural networks accept a fixed-size input and process data strictly in one direction from input to output. However, real-world data like sentences, audio, and daily time series arrive as sequential data of arbitrary length. Feedforward networks fail to capture temporal dependencies because they lack a mechanism to retain past information.

To solve this issue, **recurrent neural networks** (RNNs) incorporate feedback loops that feed a neuron's past output back into itself as an input for the next step. As **Figure 15-1** shows, unrolling a recurrent neuron across the time axis reveals that at time step $t$, it processes both the current input $\mathbf{x}_{(t)}$ and its previous output $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{(t-1)}$. When expanded to a layer of recurrent neurons (**Figure 15-2**), each neuron has two weight vectors, $\mathbf{w}_x$ for current inputs and $\mathbf{w}_{\hat{y}}$ for outputs from the previous time step, and the whole layer places all of them in two weight matrices, $\mathbf{W}_x$ and $\mathbf{W}_{\hat{y}}$. As defined in **Equation 15-1**, the single-instance output calculation is $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{(t)} = \phi(\mathbf{W}_x^\top \mathbf{x}_{(t)} + \mathbf{W}_{\hat{y}}^\top \hat{\mathbf{y}}_{(t-1)} + \mathbf{b})$.

For example, consider a single recurrent neuron with weight $w_x = 1.0$, recurrent weight $w_{\hat{y}} = 0.5$, bias $b = 0$, and identity activation function $\phi(z) = z$. At $t = 0$, given input $x_{(0)} = 2$ and initial past output $\hat{y}_{(-1)} = 0$, the output is $\hat{y}_{(0)} = (1.0 \times 2) + (0.5 \times 0) = 2.0$. At $t = 1$, given input $x_{(1)} = 3$, the output becomes $\hat{y}_{(1)} = (1.0 \times 3) + (0.5 \times 2.0) = 4.0$.

Because the recurrent output at step $t$ is recursively built on previous steps, the network acts as a **memory cell** capable of preserving historical context over time.

blocks.title: Mini-batch shapes and the four input/output shapes
blocks.content:
For a whole mini-batch (Equation 15-2), the inputs at time step $t$ form a matrix $\mathbf{X}_{(t)}$ of shape $m \times n_\text{inputs}$, where $m$ is the number of instances. $\mathbf{W}_x$ is $n_\text{inputs} \times n_\text{neurons}$, $\mathbf{W}_{\hat{y}}$ is $n_\text{neurons} \times n_\text{neurons}$, and the output $\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{(t)}$ is $m \times n_\text{neurons}$. The two weight matrices are often concatenated vertically into one matrix $\mathbf{W}$ of shape $(n_\text{inputs} + n_\text{neurons}) \times n_\text{neurons}$, and the inputs and previous outputs are concatenated horizontally.

An RNN can take four shapes. A sequence-to-sequence network outputs a sequence, such as power consumption shifted one day ahead. A sequence-to-vector network keeps only the last output, such as a sentiment score for a review. A vector-to-sequence network turns one input vector, such as an image, into a sequence like a caption. An encoder–decoder (a sequence-to-vector encoder followed by a vector-to-sequence decoder) translates much better than a single sequence-to-sequence RNN, because the last words of a sentence can affect the first words of the translation.
